findings.title: Non-git in-place path: diff/files_changed are ALWAYS empty because capture is git-only → diff-scoped QA gates silently scan nothing
findings.claim: The empty-diff-on-non-git capture behavior is REAL and traced, but it is a DOCUMENTED, INTENDED adapter limitation (git_utils.py:184 docstring; asserted by test_adapter_claude.py:591), not a silent bug. The genuine defect is the UNGUARDED DOWNSTREAM consequence: on the documented in-place fallback the diff-scoped secretscan + hallucination_guard scan zero files and record empty evidence. The capture layer behaves as specified; the pipeline lacks a degraded-mode signal so gates vacuously pass instead of flagging 'no diff signal on a non-git supported-language tree'.
findings.evidence: Code path confirmed: claude_code.py:562 `files_after = _git_porcelain_set(inv.cwd)`; :563 `files_changed = _diff_files(files_before, files_after)`; :570 `diff = _git_diff_with_untracked(inv.cwd) if files_changed else None`. git_utils.py:190-191 `if not (cwd_path / ".git").exists(): return None`; :232-234 `if before is None or after is None: return []`. So non-git ⇒ files_changed==[] ⇒ diff=None. Downstream: execute_phase.py:7383 `if developer_result is None or not developer_result.diff: return []` → secretscan_paths=[]. cwd chain verified: worktree None (non-git, 2338) → cwd_override None → effective_cwd=orch.cwd (6572) → inv.cwd=orch.cwd (6587), so the developer writes in orch.cwd and _git_porcelain_set(orch.cwd) is None. HOWEVER this empty-diff behavior is EXPLICITLY TESTED AND INTENDED at the adapter layer: tests/test_adapter_claude.py:591 `test_execute_non_git_repo_no_diff_tracking` docstring 'Without .git in cwd, files_changed should be empty and diff None' asserts exactly `files_changed==[]` and `diff is None`. git_utils.py:184 docstring 'Returns None if cwd is not a git repo ... signalling that diff tracking is not possible.' So this is a documented limitation, not a silent unintended bug at the capture layer.
findings.repro_or_probe: The finder's 'real file changed on disk but invisible' repro is weaker than claimed — test:591 uses a mock subprocess that writes nothing. Stronger probe: non-git tmp_path, adapter stub that actually writes a real file, assert files_changed==[]/diff is None (documents the limitation), THEN drive _run_qa_gates and assert secretscan/hallucination scan 0 files — that downstream vacuity is the unguarded defect to fix.

findings.title: Non-git Python repo: test_runner is VACUOUS on every task (paths=[] → 'no python changes' short-circuit), silently passing even when the developer breaks tests
findings.file_line: src/qa/test_runner.py:96-118 (_run_pytest); dispatch at src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py:7578 (run_tests(cwd, paths=secretscan_paths)); secretscan_paths from :7524
findings.claim: Confirmed exactly. On a non-git Python repo secretscan_paths is the empty LIST [] (not None), so _run_pytest hits the final else and returns passed=True 'tests: no python changes' WITHOUT invoking pytest — a silent wrong-pass on a first-class language on the documented in-place fallback. Distinct mechanism from the seed's 0-tests-collected vacuity (this is empty-changed-set, not 0 collected). A developer that breaks a test is reported green.
findings.evidence: test_runner.py:105-115 read directly: `if paths is None: targets=[]` (full suite) `else: changed_tests=[...]; if changed_tests: targets=changed_tests; elif any(p.suffix=='.py' for p in paths): targets=['tests/unit'] if ...; else: return GateResult(passed=True, details='tests: no python changes')`. Re-ran the path-selection logic over paths=[] → lands in the final else → 'RESULT: GateResult(passed=True, details="tests: no python changes") -- VACUOUS PASS'. Critically: paths is a LIST ([]) not None on the non-git path — execute_phase.py:7578 passes `paths=secretscan_paths` and 7524 `secretscan_paths = _files_changed_for_secretscan(developer_result)` which returns [] (a list) on non-git (7383-7384). So the `paths is None → full suite` branch is NEVER reached on the non-git path; it always falls to the vacuous else. pytest is never invoked.
findings.repro_or_probe: pytest: non-git tmp_path with a deliberately failing tests/test_x.py; await run_tests(tmp_path, paths=[]) currently returns passed=True 'tests: no python changes'. Fix must distinguish 'no git signal' (paths==[] because diff capture failed) from 'no python changes' and run the full suite or hard-fail rather than vacuously pass.

findings.title: Non-git in-place path has NO isolation and NO rollback: a failed/partial task's on-disk edits persist and bleed into the next task
findings.file_line: src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py:2338 (worktree only when _is_git_repo), :5349 + :5391 (apply/cleanup guarded on worktree_mgr is not None); no else-branch in-place rollback
findings.claim: Confirmed. All convergence/rollback (apply_with_conflict_escalation @5349, remove_per_task @5391, abort_failed_apply reset --hard+clean @worktree.py:979-1002, target-file reset/checkout @worktree.py:861-862) is gated on `worktree_mgr is not None` and constructed only for git repos (@2338). The non-git path (effective_cwd=orch.cwd) has NO equivalent in-place rollback/restore/snapshot. A failed/partial task's edits persist and bleed into the next task on the same orch.cwd. Bites only multi-task non-git runs.
findings.evidence: execute_phase.py:2337-2338 `worktree_mgr: WorktreeManager | None = None; if _is_git_repo(orch.cwd):` — worktree machinery only constructed for git repos. :5349 `if worktree_mgr is not None and worktree is not None: applied = await _apply_with_conflict_escalation(...)` — apply/convergence inside the git branch only. :5391 (in finally) `if worktree_mgr is not None and worktree is not None: await worktree_mgr.remove_per_task(...)` — cleanup git-only. :6572 `effective_cwd = cwd_override if cwd_override is not None else orch.cwd` (non-git → orch.cwd). worktree.py:979-1002 abort_failed_apply does `reset --hard HEAD` + scoped `clean -fd`; worktree.py:861-862 the git apply path does scoped `reset --quiet --` + `checkout --` of target files. I grep-confirmed no reset/checkout/stash/clean/snapshot exists in any worktree=None branch. The non-git path writes directly into orch.cwd with no rollback machinery.
findings.repro_or_probe: pytest/integration: non-git tmp_path, 2 dependent tasks, task 1 fails QA after writing a partial file; assert task 2's starting tree still contains task 1's partial edit (no rollback). Contrast with the git path's scoped reset at worktree.py:861-862.

findings.title: build_check Python path walks the whole tree (cwd.rglob) with only .venv/__pycache__ skipped — compiles vendored/build/node_modules .py; no _SKIP_DIRS reuse
findings.file_line: src/qa/build_check.py:81-85 (_run_python_build py_files = cwd.rglob('*.py') filtered only on '.venv'/'__pycache__')
findings.claim: Confirmed exactly. _run_python_build enumerates cwd.rglob('*.py') excluding only '.venv'/'__pycache__', so it py_compiles vendored .py under node_modules/build/dist/.tox/site-packages (proven: node_modules/dep/broken.py is included), inflating cost and surfacing third-party syntax as a build failure. Does not reuse repo_probe._SKIP_DIRS (repo_probe.py:70-83) or a git-tracked fast path. Symlink-loop hang is NOT a risk on Py3.13 (rglob no longer follows dir symlinks — verified). Cost + false-positive, not a hang.
findings.evidence: build_check.py:81-85 read directly: `py_files = [str(p) for p in cwd.rglob('*.py') if '.venv' not in p.parts and '__pycache__' not in p.parts]` — only those two dirs excluded. Real probe: /tmp/bc_probe with a.py + node_modules/dep/broken.py; the exact filter returned BOTH files, `node_modules included? True` → py_compile would surface the vendored broken.py as a 'py_compile failed'. Canonical skip set confirmed at repo_probe.py:70-83 `_SKIP_DIRS = {.git,.venv,venv,node_modules,__pycache__,.mypy_cache,.pytest_cache,dist,build,.tox}` — build_check does NOT import or reuse it. Symlink-hang ruled out: Python 3.13.5 confirmed; rglob over a self-referential dir symlink returned 1 file with no hang.
findings.repro_or_probe: pytest: tmp_path with a.py (valid) + node_modules/dep/broken.py (syntax error); await run_build_check(tmp_path, 'python') returns passed=False on the vendored broken.py. Fix = reuse _SKIP_DIRS + git-tracked fast path.

findings.title: Non-git in-place EXECUTE path is end-to-end UNTESTED (only probe_repo's os.walk fallback is covered); the wrong-pass/no-isolation bugs above are unguarded
findings.file_line: tests/test_runtime_repo_probe.py:21-33 (probe non-git dir) is the ONLY non-git coverage; no test exercises _is_git_repo→worktree_mgr=None execute path
findings.claim: Partially confirmed. The non-git EXECUTE PIPELINE (vacuous test gate, empty-evidence gate consequences, no rollback) is indeed untested end-to-end. But the finding overstated 'all four defects unguarded': the adapter-layer empty-diff contract IS guarded by test_adapter_claude.py:591 (which the finder overlooked). The real gap is narrower: the downstream gate-vacuity and no-isolation behaviors are uncovered, and detect_language has no sub-package/workspace test. Presence-anchor gates verify code exists, not that the non-git path behaves.
findings.evidence: The finder MISSED a relevant test: tests/test_adapter_claude.py:591 `test_execute_non_git_repo_no_diff_tracking` DOES drive the adapter with a non-git cwd and asserts files_changed==[]/diff is None — so the adapter-layer empty-diff behavior (the mechanism behind defect #3) IS guarded. The finder's claim 'all four non-git defects above ship unguarded' is therefore too strong. BUT the finder's core point survives: that test exercises the ADAPTER in isolation (mocked subprocess, no real file write, no gate dispatch). I confirmed via grep+inspection that NO test drives the execute_phase non-git pipeline — i.e. no test asserts the vacuous test gate (defect #4), the empty-evidence gate consequences (defect #3 downstream), or the absent rollback (defect #5). repo_probe.py:21-33 covers only probe_repo's os.walk fallback (verified, asserts file_count/is_huge). test_qa_detect: detect_language tested only at tmp_path root, no sub-package/workspace case.
findings.repro_or_probe: Add tests/test_execute_non_git_inplace.py: non-git tmp_path, stub adapter that mutates a file, drive _run_qa_gates → assert (a) the test_runner is not vacuous on a failing suite, (b) a failed task is rolled back. Plus add a detect_language sub-package/workspace descent test. test_adapter_claude.py:591 already covers the adapter empty-diff contract.

findings.title: The release gate script is NEVER invoked by any CI workflow — it is a manual local-only file; CI re-inlines anchors only through v0.36
findings.claim: ci/release_preflight_greps.sh (which holds every grep/AST presence anchor for v0.37->v0.42.1) is invoked by zero CI workflows — release.yml, test.yml, publish.yml, the Makefile, and pytest all never call it; release.yml hand-inlines grep anchors only through v0.36 D3 (line 323-329). So a regression deleting a v0.4x SYMBOL the .sh guards (e.g. the resolver module, a ledger op name) would not be caught by any workflow. IMPORTANT NUANCE the finder got wrong: the F1d AST invariant test and the resolver-engagement tests are NOT outside CI — test.yml's full `pytest tests/` runs them (verified 7 passed). The real gap is narrower than stated: it is the grep/AST *presence anchors in the .sh* (rename/deletion guards) that are ungated, not the behavioral tests.
findings.evidence: `grep -rn release_preflight_greps .github/ Makefile` -> exit 1 (no match). `grep -cE 'v0\.4' .github/workflows/release.yml` -> 0. Highest version token in release.yml = v0.36; last inlined step is 'Structural-retry routing helper (v0.36 D3)' at lines 323-329 checking should_change_model_for_class. 33 inlined `grep -` anchor steps, none for v0.37+. `grep -rln release_preflight tests/` -> none. Makefile has no preflight target. So the .sh holding ALL v0.37->v0.42.1 grep anchors runs in zero workflows — TRUE. HOWEVER the finder's collateral claim (in this finding and #3) that the F1d/engagement TESTS 'aren't in CI' is REFUTED: test.yml runs `uv run pytest tests/ -v` with `testpaths=["tests"]` and no marker-exclusion in addopts, which collects+runs tests/test_block_path_invariant.py AND tests/test_resolver_engagement.py. I ran both: `uv run pytest tests/test_block_path_invariant.py tests/test_resolver_engagement.py` -> 7 passed. So the F1d AST invariant and the resolver-engagement asserts ARE gated in CI via the full pytest job — just not via the grep-anchor .sh.
findings.repro_or_probe: Repro: `grep -rn release_preflight_greps .github/ Makefile` -> nothing; `grep -cE 'v0\.4' .github/workflows/release.yml` -> 0. Counter-evidence the script's absence is partly redundant: `uv run pytest tests/test_block_path_invariant.py tests/test_resolver_engagement.py` -> 7 passed, and test.yml runs the full suite. Fix: add `run: bash ci/release_preflight_greps.sh all` as a step in test.yml or release.yml and delete the duplicated v0.30-v0.36 inlined blocks so the .sh is the single source of truth for rename/deletion guards.

findings.title: Every v0.42/v0.42.1 resolver anchor is presence-only: the resolver can be fully INERT while all 37 anchors pass
findings.claim: The grep/AST anchors are presence-only and provably blind to runtime gating (`AUTODEV_RESOLVER_DISABLED=1` does not change the gate exit code; no anchor checks the value of `enabled`, that resolve_blocker is reached, or that any resolution op is written). The killswitch chokepoint is real (execute_phase.py:1815-1822). However the resolver CANNOT be made 'inert everywhere while every test passes' by one config flip: the production config builder default_config() (defaults.py:313) hardcodes enabled=True independently of the _default_resolver_cfg factory, and the resolver-engagement tests run in CI (test.yml full pytest) and assert the resolver actually FIRED on the default_config path. So the gate is NOT fully blind to resolver inertness — the grep anchors are blind, but the behavioral engagement tests in the same CI are not. The real weakness is that the .sh anchors give a false sense of 'verifying behavior' when they only verify symbol presence.
findings.evidence: Confirmed the grep anchors are presence-only: `bash ci/release_preflight_greps.sh v0.42` and `v0.42.1` both exit 0, and `AUTODEV_RESOLVER_DISABLED=1 bash ci/release_preflight_greps.sh v0.42` ALSO exits 0 (anchors blind to runtime gating). Killswitch chokepoint confirmed: execute_phase.py:1815-1822 `if rcfg is None or not getattr(rcfg,'enabled',False): return None` then env check at 1817. schema.py:547 `enabled: bool` (in class ResolverConfig at 523) has NO inline default. BUT the finder's specific inertness vector is REFUTED: it claims flipping `_default_resolver_cfg()` (schema.py:565) to enabled=False 'makes the resolver inert everywhere yet leaves every test green'. `_default_resolver_cfg` is only the `default_factory` (schema.py:1248) used when a legacy config.json OMITS the resolver field. The PRODUCTION/test config path is `default_config()` (defaults.py:313-318) which independently HARDCODES `resolver=ResolverConfig(enabled=True,...)`. The in-CI engagement test `test_block_task_engages_resolver_and_recovers` (test_resolver_engagement.py:122, uses cfg=default_config() at line 61) asserts `out.status != 'blocked'`, `'blocker_escalated' in ops`, `'resolution_chosen' in ops` — it FIRES the resolver and would FAIL if default_config's resolver were inert. So 'every test stays green while resolver inert' is false for the default_config path. (I could not edit defaults.py to demonstrate the flip — denied as read-only verifier — but traced the config wiring: grep confirms default_config builds the ResolverConfig directly, not via the factory.)
findings.repro_or_probe: `AUTODEV_RESOLVER_DISABLED=1 bash ci/release_preflight_greps.sh v0.42` -> exit 0 (anchors blind). Counter-evidence: test_resolver_engagement.py:122-142 asserts resolution_chosen/blocker_escalated/non-blocked using cfg=default_config(); `uv run pytest tests/test_resolver_engagement.py` -> 4 passed. Engagement check to harden the field path specifically: a test that drives a blocker through the SAME loader.py path production uses (legacy config.json with resolver omitted -> _default_resolver_cfg backfill) and asserts the resolver fires there too, since that factory IS currently untested by an engagement test.

findings.title: F1d AST invariant proves 'all blocks route through block_task' but NOT 'the resolver fires before blocking'
findings.claim: The F1d AST invariant guarantees structural routing (every blocked transition is committed inside block_task), NOT that the resolver fired first — block_task (blocker_guard.py:101-107) commits the legacy block whenever recovered is None, so F1d stays green even with a 0-fire resolver. This is accurate. But the gap is COVERED by a separate in-CI test: test_resolver_engagement.py (run by test.yml's full pytest, NOT marker-excluded) asserts the resolver actually fires and writes blocker_escalated+resolution_chosen on the default_config path. So 'the gate's strongest anchor has a semantic gap' is true of F1d alone, but the engagement guarantee is checked elsewhere in CI — the finder's claim that the firing-assert 'is NOT in CI' is incorrect.
findings.evidence: Confirmed: test_block_path_invariant.py:80-90 (test_only_block_task_commits_blocked_transition) AST-walks src/, collects every `update_task_status(...,'blocked')` site, and asserts the offender set (all sites minus {('orchestrator/blocker_guard.py','block_task')}) is empty. It checks WHERE the commit lives, never WHETHER _resolve returned a recovery — no assertion about resolver outcome. block_task (blocker_guard.py:101-107): `if recovered is not None and getattr(recovered,'status',None)!='blocked': return recovered` else `return await orch.plan_manager.update_task_status(task.id,'blocked',meta=meta or {})` — falls through to legacy block when recovered is None. So the invariant is green even with a resolver that always falls through. TRUE. HOWEVER the finder's framing that this is the 'only behavioral check and engagement test isn't in CI' is REFUTED: the sibling test_resolver_engagement.py IS in CI (test.yml full pytest, verified 7 passed total) and DOES assert firing (assert out.status != 'blocked'; blocker_escalated/resolution_chosen present). The finder's own repro acknowledges assert_no_silent_dead_ends 'is NOT in CI' — that is wrong; it runs via the full pytest job.
findings.repro_or_probe: `uv run pytest tests/test_block_path_invariant.py tests/test_resolver_engagement.py -v` -> 7 passed, including test_block_task_engages_resolver_and_recovers (asserts firing) and assert_no_silent_dead_ends invariant. To close F1d's own gap in-module (optional): add a spy on block_hook in the F1d module asserting block_task invokes the hook before committing — but the engagement file already provides this guarantee in CI.

findings.title: From the ledger alone you CANNOT reconstruct which single recovery decision fired: 6+ competing decision-op families across two parallel channels, and a disabled resolver writes nothing
findings.claim: Auditability of the recovery contract is broken from the ledger alone: there are 8 distinct decision-op families across two parallel channels (legacy ladder: recovery_hint/recovery_tier_attempted/budget_escalation/recovery_action_chosen; resolver: blocker_escalated/resolution_chosen/resolution_outcome + architect_attempt_failed). A terminal block_task commit (blocker_guard.py:105-107) writes only `meta or {}` with no decision id or preceded-by pointer. When the resolver is disabled, both record_phase_degrade (blocker_resolver.py:746-754) and the resolution_outcome emit (execute_phase.py:1890+, behind the enabled gate) write nothing, so a degrade/block carries no 'why'. There is no single canonical 'exactly one recovery decision per terminal block' record, contradicting the north-star recovery contract. Note: the in-CI assert_no_silent_dead_ends invariant only audits the resolver-ENABLED path (it checks every blocked op has a preceding blocker_escalated), so the disabled/legacy-only ledger has no equivalent runtime audit.
findings.evidence: Confirmed multiple parallel decision-op families: `grep -roE` over src/ -> recovery_action_chosen 5, recovery_tier_attempted 6, resolution_chosen 12, budget_escalation 35, recovery_hint 75, architect_attempt_failed 6, resolution_outcome 10, blocker_escalated 10 (8 families; finder said 6+, holds). Two parallel channels confirmed: legacy ladder (recovery_hint/recovery_tier_attempted/budget_escalation) vs resolver (blocker_escalated/resolution_chosen/resolution_outcome). record_phase_degrade killswitch confirmed at blocker_resolver.py:746-754: `if rcfg is None or not getattr(rcfg,'enabled',False): return` (and env check) — emits ZERO ledger ops when resolver disabled. block_task's terminal commit (blocker_guard.py:105-107) writes only `meta=meta or {}` — no decision id, no preceded-by pointer. resolution_outcome (execute_phase.py:1890-1905) is written only inside _maybe_resolve_blocker, AFTER the enabled-gate at 1815-1822, so it never fires on the disabled path. So a ledger reader has no canonical 'terminal block B was preceded by exactly decision D' record across both channels, and the disabled-resolver path leaves a bare blocked transition with no 'why'.
findings.repro_or_probe: `for op in recovery_action_chosen recovery_tier_attempted resolution_chosen budget_escalation recovery_hint architect_attempt_failed resolution_outcome blocker_escalated; do echo $op $(grep -roE $op src/|wc -l); done` -> 8 families. Probe: ledger-replay test driving N tasks to terminal blocked/degraded asserting each is preceded by exactly one decision op from a SINGLE canonical family carrying a blocker_key. Gate addition: emit a mandatory resolution_outcome (with outcome=resolver_disabled on the killswitch path) immediately before every block_task commit and every degrade, so the disabled path leaves a breadcrumb rather than silence.

findings.title: No ruff/mypy gate in ANY workflow; mypy is a declared dep but never invoked in CI
findings.claim: No ruff/mypy/flake8/pylint step exists in any of release.yml, test.yml, or publish.yml (verified `grep -rn -iE 'ruff|mypy|...' .github/workflows/` -> no match). mypy is declared as a dev dependency (pyproject.toml:57) but invoked by zero workflows; ruff is not even declared. The only non-grep, non-full-pytest behavioral CI checks are version/CHANGELOG/retrospective discipline, reviewer.md size+VERDICT sanity, and one slash-command drift test. Type/lint regressions ship unmonitored. (I did not re-count the seed's ~8 ruff/~34 mypy errors — out of read-only scope; the absence of the gate is what is verified.)
findings.evidence: `grep -rn -iE 'ruff|mypy|flake8|pylint' .github/workflows/` -> exit 1 (no match anywhere). Read all 3 workflows: test.yml runs only `uv run pytest tests/ -v`, an e2e pytest, and one drift test (test_canonical_spec_subcommands_match_cli_registry); publish.yml only builds+publishes wheel/npm; release.yml has version/CHANGELOG/retrospective/reviewer-sanity + 33 grep-anchor steps, no lint. `grep -n -iE 'mypy|ruff' pyproject.toml` -> line 57 `mypy>=1.14` (declared dev dep), and no ruff anywhere. So mypy is installed but never run in CI, ruff is neither configured nor run. Confirmed exactly as the finder states.
findings.repro_or_probe: `grep -rn -iE 'ruff|mypy|flake8|pylint' .github/workflows/` -> empty. Probe the current error counts: `uv run ruff check src/ | tail -1` and `uv run mypy src/ 2>&1 | tail -1`. Fix: add `ruff check` + `mypy` steps to test.yml (PR-blocking) with a `--no-new-errors`/baseline so the count can only decrease.

findings.title: Anchor patterns are loose substrings that match comments/docstrings — several 'behavioral' anchors are satisfiable by a comment alone
findings.claim: Many .sh anchors are bare-substring `grep -q` checks (check() at lines 17-26 has no -w/def/call anchoring), so they pass on a comment or docstring mention rather than a live code path. Concrete proof: the resolver-killswitch anchor (line 202, `AUTODEV_RESOLVER_DISABLED`) matches the COMMENT at execute_phase.py:1594 and the docstring at 1808 — deleting the actual runtime gate at 1817 would leave the anchor green. `block_task` (line 224), `record_phase_degrade` (228), `_limit(` (231), `files_referenced` (238) are similarly loose. This compounds the other findings by making the (already ungated, per #1) .sh easy to keep green while wiring rots. The mitigating fact is these are rename/deletion guards, and the behavioral guarantees live in the in-CI engagement/F1d tests, not the anchors.
findings.evidence: check() (release_preflight_greps.sh:17-26) is a plain `grep -q "$pattern" "$file"` — no -w, no def/class/call anchoring. Confirmed loose patterns: line 202 greps bare `AUTODEV_RESOLVER_DISABLED` in execute_phase.py; `grep -n AUTODEV_RESOLVER_DISABLED src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py` -> 1594 (a COMMENT: '# disabled (cfg.resolver.enabled is False / ``AUTODEV_RESOLVER_DISABLED``)'), 1808 (docstring), 1817 (the real `os.environ.get(...)` check). So the anchor passes even if the runtime check at 1817 were deleted, as long as the comment at 1594 remains. Line 224 greps bare `block_task` in execute_phase.py (satisfied by an import or comment, not the 20 real call sites — `grep -c 'block_task(' src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py` -> 20). Lines 228 (`record_phase_degrade`), 231 (`_limit(`), 238 (`files_referenced`) are likewise bare substrings. Confirmed.
findings.repro_or_probe: `grep -n AUTODEV_RESOLVER_DISABLED src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py` -> 1594 (comment), 1808 (docstring), 1817 (code) — anchor at .sh:202 would pass on the comment alone. Probe/fix: for the would-be-behavioral anchors, anchor on the runtime form (e.g. `os.environ.get("AUTODEV_RESOLVER_DISABLED"`) or reuse the test_block_path_invariant.py AST machinery to assert block_task is CALLED >=1 time; demote the schema/op-name anchors to explicit 'rename guards' and rely on the engagement tests as the real behavioral gate.

findings.title: Two-channel split: quarantine/typed-halt (rate-limit/auth/infra) is a SEPARATE recovery channel that NEVER reaches block_task or the resolver — violates the one-coherent-channel north star
findings.claim: Confirmed exactly as claimed. AuthenticationFailedError and InfrastructureCircuitOpenError caught at execute_phase.py:3448 stamp status='quarantined' via update_task_status (not block_task), bypass the resolver entirely, and re-raise to abort the run. The resolver HAS an INFRA_CIRCUIT_OPEN ladder (deterministic: fall_through, blocker_resolver.py:160-168) but the primary quarantine path at 3448-3471 never reaches it. The architect-infra path at 1525 does call block_task with INFRA_CIRCUIT_OPEN, confirming two divergent infra paths with different recovery semantics.
findings.evidence: execute_phase.py:3448 catches `(AuthenticationFailedError, InfrastructureCircuitOpenError)`, stamps `update_task_status(task.id, 'quarantined', ...)` at 3460-3464, then re-raises — never calling block_task or _maybe_resolve_blocker. `grep -n 'block_task\|_maybe_resolve_blocker' execute_phase.py | grep -E '^3[4-6][0-9][0-9]:'` returns empty (no resolver call in the quarantine region 3448-3471). The cross-task handler at 2606-2619 calls `_halt_for_auth_failed` (not block_task). blocker_guard.py:block_task (line 71-107) only ever calls `_resolve` → `_maybe_resolve_blocker`, which is the resolver path — confirming quarantine bypasses it. By contrast the architect-infra path at execute_phase.py:1525 explicitly calls block_task with INFRA_CIRCUIT_OPEN — two divergent infra paths.
findings.repro_or_probe: Raise InfrastructureCircuitOpenError from _execute_one; assert task.status=='quarantined' and no 'blocker_escalated'/'resolution_chosen' ledger op exists for it. Compare to the architect-infra path (execute_phase.py:1525) which calls block_task(failure_class=INFRA_CIRCUIT_OPEN) — one class, two paths, two terminal statuses ('quarantined' vs potential 'blocked').

findings.title: Legacy escalation ladder is precedence-PRIOR to the resolver at every per-task retry site; resolver is only reached AFTER the ladder terminates at SOFT_BLOCKER
findings.file_line: src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py:5626 (next_step fires first), 5686 (ladder dispatch), 5853 (block_task → resolver only on soft-blocker)
findings.claim: Confirmed exactly as claimed. For test-fail, reviewer-MALFORMED, and all per-task retry paths, _try_retry_or_escalate fires next_step (5626) first; REFINE returns at 5989 and PIVOT returns at 5949 without touching block_task or the resolver. The resolver is reached only via block_task at the SOFT_BLOCKER rung (5853, failure_class=SOFT_BLOCKER) and the legacy retry-exhaustion rung (6053, failure_class=UNKNOWN). The resolver is thus the LAST decision point, not the first.
findings.evidence: execute_phase.py:5626: `step = next_step(stuck_state, ...)` fires BEFORE any resolver call. Line 5686: `if step != 'continue':` dispatches ladder branches. Lines 5907-5949 (pivot) and 5985-5989 (refine) both return without calling block_task or _maybe_resolve_blocker. Only the soft-blocker branch at 5828 (`if resolution.action == 'soft-blocker':`) calls `block_task(failure_class=_fcls.SOFT_BLOCKER)` at line 5853, which reaches the resolver. The retry-exhaustion path at 6053 also calls block_task(failure_class=UNKNOWN). escalation_ladder.py:168-172 confirms SOFT_BLOCKER fires when pivot_count>=_PIVOT_SOFT_BLOCKER_THRESHOLD or architect_count>=1.

findings.title: DOUBLE-DISPATCH ordering hazard on DAG/cross-phase path: resolver runs once for the plan (task=None) then again per-task, double-counting cycle budget and emitting duplicate blocker_escalated ledger ops
findings.file_line: src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py:2491 (plan-level _maybe_resolve_blocker) + 2501 (per-task block_task→_maybe_resolve_blocker again); guard key at 1836
findings.claim: Confirmed. execute_phase.py:2491/2533 invokes _maybe_resolve_blocker with task=None (guard_key='-:dag_invalid'). Then 2501/2540 calls block_task per pending task, each of which calls _maybe_resolve_blocker with guard_key='<task.id>:dag_invalid' — a distinct key. The in-memory cycle counter (orch._resolver_cycle_counts) does not deduplicate across keys, so N+1 resolver cycles are burned and N+1 blocker_escalated/resolution_chosen/resolution_outcome triples are written. The plan-level call (task=None) emits resolution_outcome with outcome='fell_through'; per-task calls also emit fell_through.
findings.evidence: execute_phase.py:2491: `await _maybe_resolve_blocker(orch, None, failure_class='cross_phase_dag_invalid', ...)` — plan-level. execute_phase.py:2501: `await block_task(orch, t, failure_class=_fcls.CROSS_PHASE_DAG_INVALID, ...)` per pending task; blocker_guard.py:92 calls `_resolve` → `_maybe_resolve_blocker` again. Guard key at execute_phase.py:1836: `f"{task.id if task is not None else '-'}:{failure_class}"`. Plan-level key: `'-:cross_phase_dag_invalid'`; per-task keys: `'1.1:cross_phase_dag_invalid'`, `'1.2:cross_phase_dag_invalid'` etc. — ALL DIFFERENT keys, no deduplication. Each call emits its own `blocker_escalated` + `resolution_chosen` + `resolution_outcome` triple. With N pending tasks, N+1 resolver cycles are consumed for one logical failure.
findings.repro_or_probe: Inject a DAG cycle with 5 pending tasks, resolver ON; count ledger 'blocker_escalated' ops — expect 6 (1 plan-level + 5 per-task) for a single DagValidationError. Verify guard keys are distinct: `-:dag_invalid` vs `1.1:dag_invalid` etc.

findings.title: Test-diag breaker (I4 backoff) and per-task TEST_DIAGNOSIS hardfail are two mechanisms on the same class with an ordering race: cross-task halt yields 'quarantined', per-task hardfail yields 'blocked' — nondeterministic terminal for one root cause

Which fires first for a given task depends on cross-task ordering (whether enough OTHER tasks have already failed to trip the breaker's deque threshold before THIS task's second attempt completes). Same root cause (capture_failed), two possible terminal statuses ('quarantined' vs 'blocked').

findings.title: OVERLAP: GUARDRAIL_EXCEEDED resolver escalate_budget rung resets retry_count=0 with no awareness of the in-memory BudgetEscalationTracker — two budget-widening mechanisms with no shared ceiling

findings.title: LLM resolver (the whole point of ADR-0047) is reachable from only ~3 generic UNKNOWN block sites; every other terminal assigns a KNOWN class → deterministic ladder, never the LLM

findings.title: (a) Canonical action set: 5 disjoint recovery vocabularies; ResolutionActionType is the only superset — adopt it canonical with explicit per-vocabulary mapping

The schemas.py:932-944 comment documents the WITHIN-vocabulary mapping of ResolutionActionType to primitives, not a cross-vocabulary canonical mapping — the cross-vocabulary alignment noted in the corrected_claim is design intent, not existing code. choose_recovery_action is audit-only (confirmed, execute_phase.py:5653-5660 comment).

findings.title: (b) Single typed stuck signal: split across in-memory StuckState, free-text ESCALATE:, adapter subtypes, and a BlockerContext only the resolver sees — unify on BlockerContext fed the ladder trajectory

findings.title: (c) Resume-safe per-agent budget: TWO budgets, BOTH unsafe — budget_escalation tracker in-memory-only; resolver ledger budget reads 0 under a fake ledger, forcing an in-memory backstop that also resets on resume

(2) blocker_resolver.py:89-107 — count_prior_cycles reads from `ledger_mod.read_entries(orch.cwd)` (ledger-backed, resume-safe). findings.title: (d) Deps/merge ownership: deps in dag.py (pure, plan-time), merge in worktree_mgr (apply-time), but RECOVERY split across 3 vocabularies + 4 block sites — name ONE owner emitting a BlockerContext
findings.claim: Confirmed. DAG validity owned by dag.py (topological_levels:369, find_file_overlaps:475, validate_edit_scope:618). Merge recovery is decided twice: (1) conflict-critic in _apply_with_conflict_escalation uses ConflictAction {rebase-and-retry/abandon-task/rewrite} (execute_phase.py:2101-2171) BEFORE any BlockerContext; (2) the resolver's deterministic conflict ladder (blocker_resolver.py:244-269 re_architect→ask_human) handles the TERMINAL block sites CONFLICT_3WAY_FAILED/CONFLICT_ABANDON/CONFLICT_REWRITE_CAP_EXCEEDED via block_task. These two adjudications use disjoint vocabularies and share no state. The structural DAG failures (DAG_INVALID etc.) are NOT in the conflict-critic path and are separately flagged as STRUCTURAL in failure_classes.py:97-103.
findings.evidence: Four independent code checks: (1) dag.py:369,475,618 — topological_levels, find_file_overlaps, validate_edit_scope confirmed at those exact line numbers. (2) execute_phase.py:2101-2171 — _escalate_conflict_to_critic is called first (2101) and branches on ConflictAction {rebase-and-retry → 3way apply, abandon-task → block_task CONFLICT_ABANDON@2153, rewrite → retries up to cap → block_task CONFLICT_REWRITE_CAP_EXCEEDED@2171; also CONFLICT_3WAY_FAILED@2141}. This is a SEPARATE adjudication using a vocabulary disjoint from the resolver. (3) blocker_resolver.py:244-269 — resolver has its OWN conflict ladder (re_architect→ask_human) for CONFLICT_3WAY_FAILED/CONFLICT_ABANDON/CONFLICT_REWRITE_CAP_EXCEEDED. (4) failure_classes.py:97-103 — STRUCTURAL_FAILURE_CLASSES = {DAG_INVALID, CROSS_PHASE_DAG_INVALID, EDIT_SCOPE_VIOLATION, INFRA_CIRCUIT_OPEN} explicitly notes 'resolver should NOT attempt task-local recovery'. The conflict path is NOT in STRUCTURAL_FAILURE_CLASSES, so the resolver DOES attempt merge recovery but via a disjoint vocabulary from the conflict-critic.
findings.repro_or_probe: Read execute_phase.py:2101-2171 to see the conflict-critic deciding rebase/abandon/rewrite independently of BlockerContext. Then read blocker_resolver.py:244-269 to see the second conflict ladder (re_architect/ask_human). Neither informs the other — they are independent adjudications of the same merge failure. grep 'CONFLICT_3WAY_FAILED\|CONFLICT_ABANDON\|CONFLICT_REWRITE_CAP_EXCEEDED' src/orchestrator/failure_classes.py confirms these are NOT in STRUCTURAL_FAILURE_CLASSES.

findings.title: (e) Resolver insertion point: move the chokepoint to the TOP of _try_retry_or_escalate (before next_step @~5626), not after the legacy SOFT_BLOCKER rung (5853) — today it is the last rung AND its structural actions are inert by construction
findings.file_line: src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py:5626 (next_step call), 5792-5802 (ARCHITECT_CONSULT returns without block_task), 5828-5905 (soft-blocker→block_task@5853), 5907-5949 (pivot returns without block_task), 5951-5989 (refine returns without block_task), 6053 (retry-exhaustion→block_task UNKNOWN); src/orchestrator/blocker_resolver.py:244-391 (structural action rationale prose, no 'direction' param); src/orchestrator/corrective_parser.py:79-82 (empty return on no-bullet text)
findings.claim: Confirmed exactly as stated. The resolver chokepoint (_maybe_resolve_blocker→block_task) is reached at ONLY TWO points in _try_retry_or_escalate: (a) when the critic returns 'soft-blocker' (execute_phase.py:5853) and (b) after legacy retry-limit exhaustion (6053, with failure_class=UNKNOWN). REFINE (5907-5949), PIVOT (5951-5989), and ARCHITECT_CONSULT (5792-5802) all return without calling block_task, so the resolver never sees them. For structural failure classes (re_architect, re_plan, split_task, narrow_scope), blocker_resolver.py's _act() never passes a 'direction' param (grep confirms 0 hits), so _apply_resolution falls back to the prose rationale string, which has no top-level bullet markers, causing parse_corrective_direction to return [] and _resolver_corrective to return None — the resolver fires but recovers nothing. The proposed fix (move the call to before next_step + pass structured corrective_tasks param, not prose) is the correct direction.
findings.evidence: Five independent traces: (1) execute_phase.py:5626 — `step = next_step(stuck_state, ...)` fires first; (2) ARCHITECT_CONSULT at 5792 returns `arch_resolution` at 5802 without reaching block_task; (3) critic 'pivot' branch at 5907 returns at 5949 (`return await orch.plan_manager.get_task(task.id) or task`) — no block_task; (4) critic 'refine' branch at 5951 returns at 5989 — no block_task; (5) ONLY `resolution.action == 'soft-blocker'` (5828) routes to block_task at 5853, and the legacy 'continue' path hits block_task at 6053 with failure_class=_fcls.UNKNOWN. For the inertness sub-claim: `grep -n "'direction'" src/orchestrator/blocker_resolver.py` returns 0 hits — _act() never passes direction= in any call. So _apply_resolution at execute_phase.py:1764 always evaluates `params.get('direction') or rationale`, falling through to the prose rationale string. corrective_parser.py:79-82 returns [] for any text with no top-level bullet (confirmed: `if not text or not text.strip(): return []` then splits on _RE_TOP_LEVEL_BULLET=`^[ ]?(?:[-*]|\d+\.)\s+(.+)$`). Prose rationales from blocker_resolver.py (e.g. 'merge conflict could not be resolved mechanically: rethink the task at component altitude') contain no leading `- ` or `* ` or `1.` bullets → 0 tasks → _resolver_corrective returns None → legacy block.
findings.repro_or_probe: grep -n "'direction'" src/orchestrator/blocker_resolver.py → 0 hits (proves no direction param in any deterministic action). Then: python3 -c "import sys;sys.path.insert(0,'src');from orchestrator.corrective_parser import parse_corrective_direction;print(parse_corrective_direction('merge conflict could not be resolved mechanically: rethink the task at component altitude so the patches stop colliding.',phase_id='1',base_task_count=0))" → [] (proves 0 corrective tasks from prose). Field trace: with resolver enabled, drive a task to CONFLICT_3WAY_FAILED and confirm ledger shows resolution_chosen(action=re_architect) followed immediately by resolution_outcome(outcome=fell_through).

findings.title: Cascade-block (`mark_blocked_descendants`) commits terminal `blocked` via direct attribute assignment — bypasses both block_task/resolver AND the AST CI gate
findings.claim: Confirmed exactly as stated. `mark_blocked_descendants` (plan_manager.py:990-1044) sets `t.status = "blocked"` directly at line 1019 for every pending descendant. This never calls `block_task` (orchestrator/blocker_guard.py), so these descendant blocks route through zero resolver logic. The v0.42.1 AST gate (`_block_sites()` in test_block_path_invariant.py:47-77) only parses `ast.Call` nodes named `update_task_status` — structurally blind to `ast.Assign` attribute writes — so `pytest tests/test_block_path_invariant.py` is 3/3 green despite the bypass existing.
findings.evidence: plan_manager.py:1019 is `t.status = "blocked"  # type: ignore[assignment]` — a direct ast.Assign to an attribute, never calling block_task or update_task_status. The AST gate in tests/test_block_path_invariant.py:57-77 walks only `ast.Call` nodes named `update_task_status`, so it is structurally blind to any `ast.Assign`/`ast.AnnAssign` to `.status`. Running `pytest tests/test_block_path_invariant.py -q` prints `3 passed` — the gate is green while plan_manager.py:1019 is live. There are 5 total direct `.status = "blocked"` assignments in src/: plan_manager.py:1019 (live cascade-block), plan_manager.py:1585 (ledger replay op `mark_blocked`), plan_manager.py:1674 (ledger replay op `mark_blocked_descendants`), ledger.py:1302 (replay), ledger.py:1434 (replay). The live site at 1019 is the confirmed bypass; the other four are ledger-replay state reconstruction.
findings.repro_or_probe: Add `.status = "blocked"` to any src/ file and run `pytest tests/test_block_path_invariant.py` — it still passes, proving the gate is blind. Or directly: `grep -rn '.status = "blocked"' src/ | grep -v __pycache__` returns 5 hits; none are caught by the gate. Gate fix: extend `_block_sites()` to also walk `ast.Assign`/`ast.AugAssign` nodes whose target is `Attribute(attr='status')` with value `ast.Constant('blocked')`.

findings.title: Two of three cascade-block sites also leave the FAILED PARENT un-routed through block_task (no resolver for the parent either)
findings.claim: The in-phase (3048-3067) and cross-phase (3336-3354) defensive nets only cascade-block descendants without calling `block_task` for the parent. However, these defensive nets only fire if `_execute_one_worker`'s own `except Exception` (line 3472) itself raises — which is an edge case, not the normal path. In normal operation the parent IS routed through `block_task` at line 3566 inside `_execute_one_worker`. The real risk is: if `block_task` or `mark_blocked_descendants` raises inside `_execute_one_worker`, the parent leaks in an indeterminate status and the downstream defensive net handles only the descendants with no resolver path for the parent. The claim that the parent is 'never routed through block_task' is overstated; 'never routed through block_task in the defensive-net path' is accurate.
findings.evidence: Confirmed: in-phase net (3048-3067) and cross-phase net (3336-3354) call only `mark_blocked_descendants` for descendants — never `block_task` for the parent `finished_id`. However, the finding overstates the practical risk. `_execute_one_worker` (the asyncio task submitted to the pool) has its own `except Exception` at line 3472 that catches all non-auth/infra exceptions, calls `block_task` for the parent (line 3566), and RETURNS (does not re-raise). So in normal operation the parent IS routed through `block_task` by `_execute_one_worker` — the pool dispatcher's `d.result()` at 2988 gets the returned blocked Task. The defensive nets at 3048/3336 only fire if `_execute_one_worker`'s own catch block fails (e.g., `block_task` raises internally), which would leave the parent in an indeterminate state. The auth/infra exceptions (which do re-raise from `_execute_one_worker`) are handled at 2990/3285 separately, not at 3048/3336. The structural gap is real; the practical frequency is low.
findings.repro_or_probe: To hit the gap: monkeypatch `block_task` to raise inside `_execute_one_worker`'s `except Exception` handler; verify the pool dispatcher's defensive net at 3048 fires and calls `mark_blocked_descendants` for descendants but the parent's status is unresolved. Confirm by inspecting the plan state: parent task status is still whatever `_execute_one` left it before the exception.

findings.title: `quarantined` is an alternate terminal-equivalent halt that bypasses block_task and the resolver for the entire infra/auth failure class
findings.claim: Confirmed exactly as stated. `AuthenticationFailedError`/`InfrastructureCircuitOpenError` at the per-task worker level stamp `quarantined` via `update_task_status` directly (never `block_task`), then re-raise to abort the phase. This bypasses the ADR-0047 resolver entirely for the infra/auth failure class on the dominant (per-task) path. The inconsistency with the architect-consult infra path (execute_phase.py:1525 which DOES call `block_task(INFRA_CIRCUIT_OPEN)`) is confirmed: two infra-circuit paths, one resolver-routed, one not. The code's defense ('quarantined is non-terminal, resume picks it up') is valid but does not provide resolver-breadcrumbed recovery decisions.
findings.evidence: execute_phase.py:3448: `except (AuthenticationFailedError, InfrastructureCircuitOpenError) as exc:` → 3460-3464: `await orch.plan_manager.update_task_status(task.id, "quarantined", ...)` + `raise` at 3471 — never calls `block_task`. `_halt_task_for_auth_failed` at 2668-2699: similarly stamps `quarantined` directly via `update_task_status`. `_TERMINAL_TASK_STATUSES` at line 101 = `("complete", "blocked", "skipped")` — `quarantined` is absent. By contrast, the architect-consult infra path at execute_phase.py:1525-1537 calls `block_task(..., failure_class=_fcls.INFRA_CIRCUIT_OPEN)` — routing through the resolver for the same class. So two different code paths for the same exception type produce inconsistent behavior: one resolves via `block_task` (architect path) and one bypasses it entirely (per-task worker path). The `quarantined` path never emits `blocker_escalated`/`resolution_chosen` ledger ops.
findings.repro_or_probe: Raise `InfrastructureCircuitOpenError` from inside `_execute_one` (any point before the auth/infra catch at 3448); assert `task.status == 'quarantined'`, `_maybe_resolve_blocker` invoked 0 times, ledger has NO `blocker_escalated`/`resolution_chosen` op. Then compare to the architect-consult infra path (execute_phase.py:1507-1537) which calls `block_task(INFRA_CIRCUIT_OPEN)` and DOES emit those ledger ops — demonstrating the inconsistency.

findings.title: AST gate cannot inspect variable (non-Constant) status args — a future `target = "blocked"` refactor slips past CI silently
findings.claim: Confirmed exactly as stated. The AST gate only catches `update_task_status` calls where the status arg is a literal `ast.Constant` string equal to `'blocked'`. Three live call sites already use non-Constant (variable) status args at execute_phase.py:1545, 1666, and ~7261. Currently these variables resolve to non-blocked values at runtime. The structural blindness means a maintainer could write `target_status = "blocked"` and `update_task_status(task.id, target_status)` — bypassing `block_task` — and the CI gate would pass green. Additionally, the gate is also blind to direct `.status = "blocked"` attribute assignments (5 live in src/; see finding 1).
findings.evidence: test_block_path_invariant.py:69-76: the gate records a block site only when `node.args[1]` is `isinstance(..., ast.Constant)` with `.value == 'blocked'`, or when a keyword `status=` has `isinstance(kw.value, ast.Constant)` with `.value == 'blocked'`. execute_phase.py:1544: `target_status = "in_progress" if task.status != "in_progress" else task.status` then `update_task_status(task.id, target_status, ...)` — `target_status` is a variable, not a Constant. Line 1665: `target = "in_progress" if ...` — same pattern. Line ~7261: `for _status in ("coded", "auto_gated", ...): ... update_task_status(task.id, _status)` — `_status` is a loop variable. All three are currently safe (they only assign non-blocked statuses at runtime), but the gate is structurally blind to any variable-routed status — including future `target_status = "blocked"` refactors. The gate test passes (3/3 green) with these live variable sites.
findings.repro_or_probe: Add `target = "blocked"; await pm.update_task_status(task.id, target)` in any src/ file and run `pytest tests/test_block_path_invariant.py` — it passes. Fix: either (a) extend `_block_sites()` to also flag variable-status `update_task_status` calls as 'requires allowlist review', or (b) rename the canonical status string to a sentinel that only `block_task` imports, making it impossible to pass as a variable without importing the sentinel.

findings.title: Direct cascade-block assignment also bypasses the FSM transition guard (assert_transition), not just the resolver
findings.claim: Confirmed structurally: the direct assignment at plan_manager.py:1019 bypasses `assert_transition`, which is enforced by the canonical `update_task_status` at line 350. No illegal transition occurs today because the pending-filter at line 999 ensures only `pending` descendants are touched and `pending -> blocked` is legal (task_state.py:42). The risk is future-oriented: if the filter widens to include other statuses, there is no FSM guard protecting the assignment. The severity of this finding is primarily as an additional argument for routing through `update_task_status` (or `block_task`) rather than as a live bug.
findings.evidence: plan_manager.py:350: `assert_transition(task.status, status)` — every `update_task_status` call enforces the state machine. plan_manager.py:1019: `t.status = "blocked"` directly — no `assert_transition` call. The filter at plan_manager.py:999 (`if t.status == "pending"`) ensures only pending descendants are touched; `pending -> blocked` is a legal edge in `TASK_TRANSITIONS` (task_state.py:42). So NO illegal transition currently occurs. The risk is purely structural/forward-looking: if the pending-filter at 999 is ever widened (e.g., also blocking `in_progress` descendants), the direct write at 1019 would silently permit a potentially-illegal transition (e.g., `in_progress -> blocked` IS legal at task_state.py:43, but other future statuses might not be). The claim that 'pending -> blocked is a legal edge' is confirmed at task_state.py:42.
findings.repro_or_probe: Unit test: call `mark_blocked_descendants` after artificially setting a descendant to `in_progress` status via a crafted plan object (bypassing the pending-filter at 999); observe the write silently succeeds (no ValueError) because there is no `assert_transition` at 1019. `in_progress -> blocked` is actually legal (task_state.py:43), so demonstrate with a hypothetical future status: add `'tested'` to the pending-filter, verify `tested -> blocked` IS legal (task_state.py:62) — so today the risk is theoretical unless a truly non-legal transition is reached.

findings.title: Budget-escalation counter is in-memory only; the paired ladder counter (task.retry_count) is PERSISTED — NOT resume-safe, defeating the feature's stated purpose on every restart
findings.file_line: src/orchestrator/budget_escalation.py:33-36,179 (_counters dict, docstring 'NOT persisted across resume, by design'); src/orchestrator/__init__.py:249-251 (BudgetEscalationTracker() constructed empty per Orchestrator); src/state/schemas.py:256 (retry_count IS a persisted Task field); src/state/plan_manager.py:1221-1235 (mark_task_retry persists retry_count to ledger+snapshot)
findings.claim: Confirmed exactly as stated. BudgetEscalationTracker._counters is an in-memory dict built empty on every Orchestrator instantiation and never written to ledger or disk. task.retry_count is a persisted Task field written via mark_task_retry to the ledger and plan.json snapshot. After a restart, the budget escalation ladder resets to attempt=0 (base budget, no bump) even though task.retry_count proves the task already exhausted its turn budget N times. The stated docstring explicitly calls this 'by design' but it means consecutive error_max_turns across a restart never escalates budget.
findings.evidence: budget_escalation.py lines 33-36 read: 'the orchestrator instance is replaced (in-memory only — NOT persisted across resume, by design — repeated max-turns in a fresh session starts the escalation ladder over)'. BudgetEscalationTracker dataclass at line 179 has `_counters: dict[tuple[str, str], int] = field(default_factory=dict)`. __init__.py:251 constructs `BudgetEscalationTracker()` empty. schemas.py:256 shows `retry_count: int = 0` is a plain field on Task, persisted via plan_manager.py:1221-1235 which calls append_entry + snapshot_plan with retry_count.
findings.repro_or_probe: python -c "from orchestrator.budget_escalation import BudgetEscalationTracker as B; t=B(); t.record_result('1.1','developer','error_max_turns'); t.record_result('1.1','developer','error_max_turns'); print('proc1',t.current_attempt('1.1','developer')); print('resume',B().current_attempt('1.1','developer'))" -> prints proc1 2 / resume 0.

findings.title: Seed under-counts: there are THREE independent retry counters for one failing task, with mixed persistence and NO shared reset — the divergence is worse than 'two counters'
findings.file_line: src/state/plan_manager.py:1221 (task.retry_count, PERSISTED via mark_task_retry+snapshot); src/orchestrator/budget_escalation.py:179,250 (_counters, in-memory); src/state/plan_manager.py:1070-1090,122 (StuckState.discard_count, in-memory, 'NOT persisted'); src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py:5985-5989,5945-5949 (REFINE/PIVOT restart WITHOUT calling mark_task_retry)
findings.claim: Confirmed. Three counters track the same failing task: task.retry_count (persisted, bumped ONLY on the legacy 'continue' path via mark_task_retry at 5992), BudgetEscalationTracker._counters (in-memory, reset on any non-error_max_turns), StuckState.discard_count (in-memory, bumped on every _try_retry_or_escalate call including REFINE/PIVOT). REFINE at discard_count=3 restarts the task WITHOUT calling mark_task_retry, so retry_count freezes while discard_count and possibly the budget counter keep climbing.
findings.evidence: plan_manager.py:114-122 confirms _stuck_state is in-memory only. execute_phase.py:5985-5989 shows REFINE path calls update_task_status('in_progress') and returns WITHOUT calling mark_task_retry. The legacy 'continue' path at 5992 is the ONLY site calling mark_task_retry. budget_escalation.py:248-253 shows record_result increments only on 'error_max_turns', clearing on any other subtype. Three counters: (1) task.retry_count - persisted, bumped only on legacy 'continue' path; (2) BudgetEscalationTracker._counters - in-memory; (3) StuckState.discard_count - in-memory, bumped on every _try_retry_or_escalate call regardless of path taken.
findings.repro_or_probe: Write a test: drive a task through 3 error_max_turns where next_step returns REFINE at discard_count=3; assert task.retry_count stays 0 (frozen) while tracker.current_attempt==3 and stuck_state.discard_count==3 — three different values for the same task.

findings.title: Budget-escalation EXHAUSTION branch (is_exhausted -> hard-fail) is structurally unreachable at both production scopes under default config
findings.file_line: src/orchestrator/budget_escalation.py:198-205 (is_exhausted: counter > 2); src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py:6504-6515 (is_exhausted check); src/orchestrator/plan_phase.py:78,890 (_MAX_ARCHITECT_ATTEMPTS=3, range(3)); grep -rn 'is_exhausted' src/ → only execute_phase.py:6504
findings.claim: For plan_phase: CONFIRMED UNREACHABLE — is_exhausted is never called in plan_phase.py; the range(3) loop exits after 3 dispatches before a 4th could trip exhaustion. For execute_phase: REACHABLE in principle — is_exhausted is checked at 6504 before every delegate() call, and if the developer consistently returns error_max_turns through REFINE/PIVOT diversions (which re-dispatch without resetting the budget counter), counter can reach 3. However, the discard ladder's REFINE/PIVOT diversions inject different guidance that in practice breaks consecutive error_max_turns chains, making execute-phase exhaustion rare not impossible.
findings.evidence: `grep -rn 'is_exhausted' src/` returns ONLY execute_phase.py:6504 — is_exhausted is NEVER called in plan_phase.py. plan_phase.py line 890 shows `for attempt in range(_MAX_ARCHITECT_ATTEMPTS)` = range(3), giving exactly 3 dispatches (attempt 0,1,2). Counter can reach 3 after all 3 fail with error_max_turns, but the loop exits before is_exhausted is ever checked. For execute_phase, is_exhausted IS called at 6504, and the test test_escalation_caps_after_three_bumps at line 364 confirms it fires when delegate() is called directly 4 times. The finding overstates 'structurally unreachable' for execute_phase: the discard ladder REFINE/PIVOT still re-dispatch the developer, and if the developer consistently returns error_max_turns through those diversions, the counter can reach 3. The 'rarely' qualifier in the finding text is more accurate.
findings.repro_or_probe: For plan_phase: grep -n 'is_exhausted' src/orchestrator/plan_phase.py → empty. For execute_phase: run test_escalation_caps_after_three_bumps which confirms exhaustion fires at the delegate() level. The gap is that no test exercises _execute_one where the discard ladder and budget tracker interact.

findings.title: Budget-exhaustion synthetic failure is absorbed by the discard ladder rather than terminating — two recovery channels stacked on the same task
findings.claim: Confirmed exactly. When is_exhausted fires, delegate() returns a synthetic AgentResult(success=False, subtype='error_max_turns_escalation_exhausted') which falls through the developer failure path at 4418 and hits _try_retry_or_escalate at 4474. The discard ladder then decides whether to REFINE, PIVOT, or SOFT_BLOCKER — it is the actual channel that terminates. The budget hard-fail is a redundant gate that feeds into the same ladder it was supposed to supercede.
findings.evidence: execute_phase.py:6509-6515 returns AgentResult(success=False, subtype='error_max_turns_escalation_exhausted') from delegate(). This result flows to the caller at line 4375 as developer_result. Line 4418 `if not developer_result.success:` is True (success=False). Lines 4451-4473 check for sparse expansion (likely not triggered). Line 4474 calls `_try_retry_or_escalate(orch, task, retry_limit, reason=...)` — the same path as any other developer failure. The budget-escalation 'hard fail' is therefore absorbed by the discard-count ladder, which may re-dispatch or escalate via REFINE/PIVOT/SOFT_BLOCKER. The `error_max_turns_escalation_exhausted` subtype is only special-cased in _TURN_EXHAUSTION_SUBTYPES (line 7119) for the reviewer disambiguation path, never for developer-loop termination.
findings.repro_or_probe: Drive delegate() to is_exhausted with 3 consecutive error_max_turns, then confirm the returned AgentResult with subtype='error_max_turns_escalation_exhausted' causes _try_retry_or_escalate to be called (discard_count++) rather than returning the task as blocked immediately.

findings.title: Plan-phase and execute-phase share ONE tracker instance keyed only by scope string; a literal task_id of 'plan_phase' would collide the architect ladder with that task's ladder
findings.file_line: src/orchestrator/plan_phase.py:887 (_PLAN_PHASE_SCOPE = 'plan_phase') + src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py:6504,6517,6654 (scope_id = envelope.task_id) — both read/write the same orch._budget_escalation_tracker; src/orchestrator/__init__.py:249-251 (single shared tracker)
findings.claim: Confirmed. A shared BudgetEscalationTracker uses composite key (scope_id, role) with no prefix separation between plan_phase and execute_phase scopes. A plan containing a task with id='plan_phase' and role='architect' would share a counter with the plan-phase architect ladder. Task IDs are model-generated strings, so 'plan_phase' is unlikely but not impossible. The actual collision semantics: whichever caller increments the counter last would cause the other to see an inflated or reset counter.
findings.evidence: __init__.py:249-251 creates a single BudgetEscalationTracker. plan_phase.py:887 sets _PLAN_PHASE_SCOPE = 'plan_phase'. execute_phase.py:6653-6654 uses envelope.task_id as the scope key. Task IDs are in format 'phase.sequence' (e.g. '1.1') per schemas.py:176. The scope key collision on ('plan_phase', 'architect') is structurally possible if an LLM-generated plan contains a task with id='plan_phase'. Low but non-zero probability — the key space is un-namespaced.

findings.title: Escalation bump tiers (attempt 1: 1.5x/+25%, attempt 2: 2.0x/+50%) DO fire — positive control scoping the inertness findings to the resume boundary and the 4th tier only

findings.title: The critic OWNS the merge/conflict decision; the ADR-0047 resolver only sees a conflict AFTER the critic's ladder is fully exhausted (and even then is inert)
findings.file_line: src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py:2101 (_escalate_conflict_to_critic called first on WorktreeError); 2141/2153/2171 (block_task on three terminal branches)
findings.claim: The critic OWNS the merge/conflict decision with a SINGLE CALL per apply attempt (not a 'ladder'). On WorktreeError, _escalate_conflict_to_critic (line 2101) fires first and its response (rebase-and-retry/abandon-task/rewrite) fully determines the path before block_task is reached. The resolver is only invoked inside block_task at the three terminal branches (3way_failed:2141, abandon:2153, rewrite_cap_exceeded:2171) — AFTER the critic's options are spent. On the rewrite path the critic can fire up to _CONFLICT_REWRITE_RETRY_CAP=2 rounds (line 2052) before the cap triggers block_task. The resolver cannot influence merge strategy; and even at the terminal block it is inert (re_architect prose -> 0 corrective tasks).
findings.evidence: Read execute_phase.py:2080-2214. On WorktreeError, _escalate_conflict_to_critic is called at line 2101 BEFORE any block_task. The three block_task sites (2141 CONFLICT_3WAY_FAILED, 2153 CONFLICT_ABANDON, 2171 CONFLICT_REWRITE_CAP_EXCEEDED) are reached only after the critic's one-shot decision is already acted on. block_task internally calls _resolve->_maybe_resolve_blocker (blocker_guard.py:92-100), but the resolver never influences the rebase/abandon/rewrite choice — the critic's response is the sole gate. Minor imprecision in the title: the critic does NOT have a 'ladder'; it has a single call per apply attempt with the rewrite branch allowing up to _CONFLICT_REWRITE_RETRY_CAP=2 (line 2052) rounds. The 'even then is inert' claim is confirmed by the re_architect probe in Finding 2.
findings.repro_or_probe: Read execute_phase.py:2080-2214. Trace: (1) WorktreeError -> _escalate_conflict_to_critic called at 2101 with NO resolver involvement; (2) branch on resolution.action (critic's sole decision); (3) block_task only at 2141/2153/2171. To confirm inertness: python3 -c "import sys;sys.path.insert(0,'src');from orchestrator import blocker_resolver as br,failure_classes as fc;from state.schemas import BlockerContext;ctx=BlockerContext(failure_class=fc.CONFLICT_3WAY_FAILED,raw_error='x',task_id='1.1',phase_id='p1');a=br.deterministic_action(ctx);print(a.action,a.params)" -> 're_architect {}' (prose only, no direction param).

findings.title: Even after the critic exhausts, the resolver's conflict ladder is INERT by construction: re_architect feeds prose with no bullets into a bullet-only corrective parser -> 0 tasks -> fall-through to legacy block
findings.file_line: src/orchestrator/blocker_resolver.py:244-256 (re_architect rung for all conflict classes); src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py:1763-1765 (_apply_resolution maps re_architect -> _resolver_corrective); src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py:1706-1714 (_resolver_corrective calls parse_corrective_direction); src/orchestrator/corrective_parser.py:32 (_RE_BULLET)
findings.claim: Confirmed exactly as stated. For all three conflict failure classes, deterministic_action returns re_architect with params={} and a prose rationale. _apply_resolution maps re_architect to _resolver_corrective, which feeds the prose rationale (no top-level bullet markers) to parse_corrective_direction, which returns [] because _RE_BULLET requires ^[-*] or digit-dot markers. _resolver_corrective returns None -> fall-through to legacy block. The second rung (ask_human) also returns None at _apply_resolution:1761. Both rungs of the conflict resolver ladder are structurally inert: the resolver is engaged (resolution_chosen written) but the task always blocks.
findings.evidence: Verified via code read and live probe. blocker_resolver.py:244-256: all three conflict failure classes (CONFLICT_3WAY_FAILED, CONFLICT_ABANDON, CONFLICT_REWRITE_CAP_EXCEEDED) map to re_architect rung with params={} and rationale='merge conflict could not be resolved mechanically: rethink the task at component altitude so the patches stop colliding.' execute_phase.py:1763-1765: re_architect -> _resolver_corrective(orch, task, direction) where direction=str(params.get('direction') or rationale or '') = prose string. _resolver_corrective:1706 calls parse_corrective_direction(direction, ...). corrective_parser.py:32: _RE_BULLET=re.compile(r'^(?:[-*]|\d+\.)\s+(.+)$'). Live run: parse_corrective_direction('merge conflict could not be resolved mechanically: rethink the task at component altitude so the patches stop colliding.', phase_id='p1', base_task_count=1, max_tasks=8) -> [] (length 0). _resolver_corrective:1713-1714: if not corrective_tasks: return None -> fall-through to legacy block. Second rung ask_human: _apply_resolution:1761 returns None for ask_human. Both rungs are no-ops.
findings.repro_or_probe: python3 -c "import sys;sys.path.insert(0,'src');from orchestrator.corrective_parser import parse_corrective_direction;print(len(parse_corrective_direction('merge conflict could not be resolved mechanically: rethink the task at component altitude so the patches stop colliding.',phase_id='p1',base_task_count=1,max_tasks=8)))" -> 0. Fix: have deterministic_action for conflict classes emit params['direction'] as a bulleted re-plan, or add a structural-replan path in _apply_resolution that dispatches an architect call rather than parsing bullets.

findings.title: The critic's merge adjudication (rebase/abandon/rewrite) is INVISIBLE to the ledger — no ledger_append, no mark_escalated, no recovery_hint across the entire conflict region
findings.claim: Confirmed exactly as stated. The conflict-escalation loop (execute_phase.py:2080-2214) emits zero ledger ops for the critic decision. The three block_task meta dicts carry only 'blocked_reason'. There is no ledger record of: (a) that the critic was consulted, (b) what it said (rebase/abandon/rewrite), (c) how many rewrite rounds ran, or (d) which files collided. The only structured trace is logger.warning/logger.info calls (unstructured, not queryable via ledger). The resolver's resolution_outcome only fires if the resolver is enabled and records 'fell_through' — not the critic's actual recommendation.
findings.evidence: Read execute_phase.py:2080-2214 and grep confirmed: `awk 'NR>=2080 && NR<=2214' src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py | grep -c 'ledger_append\|mark_escalated\|recovery_hint'` -> 0. The entire conflict loop contains only logger.warning/logger.info calls and the three block_task calls whose meta dicts only carry 'blocked_reason' (lines 2146-2148, 2158-2160, 2176-2178) — no 'recovery_hint' key. Compare: architect-consult (execute_phase.py:1405/1423) and guardrail blocks (1511/1535) DO emit recovery_hint. The resolver's resolution_outcome op at execute_phase.py:1898 fires inside block_task/resolve_blocker only when the resolver is enabled — and even then records 'fell_through' (action=ask_human/fall_through), not the critic's decision.
findings.repro_or_probe: Drive a conflict to abandon-task in a test with a real PlanManager ledger (use the existing StubAdapter pattern): assert the ledger contains NO op with type in ('critic_conflict_decision', 'conflict_escalated') and that the blocked task meta has no 'recovery_hint' key. grep -n 'recovery_hint' src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py | grep -E '^2[01][0-9][0-9]:' -> no output.

findings.title: _escalate_conflict_to_critic is a STATELESS one-shot per apply attempt — it threads no ladder state (recovery_already_tried / failure_class / cycle counter), so it cannot coordinate with the resolver ladder and cannot self-bound across re-entries
findings.file_line: src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py:711-730 (DelegationEnvelope has only task_id + conflict_context_marker); 2080 (rewrite_rounds=0, function-scope local reset per call)
findings.claim: Confirmed exactly as stated. _escalate_conflict_to_critic builds a DelegationEnvelope with only task_id and conflict_context_marker — no attempt history, no ladder state. rewrite_rounds is a function-scope local at line 2080, reset to 0 on every call to _apply_with_conflict_escalation. On task re-entry after reaper revert, the conflict loop restarts from round 0 with no memory that the critic already adjudicated. The resolver's own _resolver_cycle_counts guard does NOT cover the critic escalation loop.
findings.evidence: Read execute_phase.py:674-730. The DelegationEnvelope at lines 711-723 has context={'task_id': task.id, 'conflict_context_marker': True} — no recovery_already_tried, failure_class, attempt_history, or cycle counter. Compare: the resolver's BlockerContext (execute_phase.py:1860-1869) threads recovery_already_tried=_prior_resolution_actions(...) for ladder advancement. Read execute_phase.py:2055-2080: rewrite_rounds=0 is initialized at line 2080 as a function-scope local, reset to 0 on every fresh _apply_with_conflict_escalation call. The resolver's cross-re-entry budget (_resolver_cycle_counts at execute_phase.py:1834-1846) guards only the resolver path (inside block_task), not the critic-escalation loop. A task reverted by the reaper and re-dispatched re-enters _apply_with_conflict_escalation with rewrite_rounds=0 and a stateless critic call.
findings.repro_or_probe: Read execute_phase.py:711-723 and 2080. Add a test: stub the critic to always return 'rewrite'; force a persistent conflict; run _apply_with_conflict_escalation twice (simulating re-entry after reaper revert); assert the developer adapter is invoked _CONFLICT_REWRITE_RETRY_CAP (=2) times PER entry (total 4 invocations), proving no cross-entry memory. Compare with the resolver's _prior_resolution_actions() which does persist across re-entries via the ledger.

findings.title: Parser fail-open biases conflicts toward abandon: an empty/garbled critic response yields ConflictResolution(action='abandon-task'), terminally blocking the task without retry
findings.file_line: src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py:131 (ConflictResolution default action='abandon-task'); 653-658 (_parse_conflict_resolution empty/no-match fallback); 730 (_escalate_conflict_to_critic returns _parse_conflict_resolution(result.text or ''))
findings.claim: Confirmed exactly as stated. ConflictResolution defaults to action='abandon-task' (line 131). _parse_conflict_resolution returns ConflictResolution() on empty string (653-654) or no RESOLUTION: directive match (657-658). A critic that times out, returns empty, or emits prose without the exact ^RESOLUTION: ...$  line causes the conflict loop to take the abandon-task branch (line 2152) and terminally block. There is no retry of the critic and no rebase-and-retry attempt on a parse miss. The most destructive of the three actions is the fail-open default.
findings.evidence: Read execute_phase.py:120-132: ConflictResolution dataclass has action: ConflictAction = 'abandon-task' at line 131. Read lines 640-671 (_parse_conflict_resolution): line 653-654 `if not critic_response: return ConflictResolution()` (default abandon-task); line 657-658 `if not matches: return ConflictResolution()` (default abandon-task). Line 730: `return _parse_conflict_resolution(result.text or '')` — an empty result.text also hits the default. Tested manually: _parse_conflict_resolution('') -> action='abandon-task'; _parse_conflict_resolution('I think you should rebase') -> action='abandon-task' (no RESOLUTION: directive). There is no critic retry on a parse miss — the first and only critic call's parse-miss goes straight to block_task(CONFLICT_ABANDON).
findings.repro_or_probe: python3 -c "import sys;sys.path.insert(0,'src');from orchestrator.execute_phase import _parse_conflict_resolution;print(_parse_conflict_resolution('').action);print(_parse_conflict_resolution('I think you should rebase').action)" -> both print 'abandon-task'. Fix: change the fail-open default to 'rebase-and-retry' (the least-destructive option), or add a critic retry (1 time) before committing to abandon.

findings.title: Escalation-ladder StuckState is in-memory-only — every counter (discard/pivot/search/architect) resets to 0 on resume, so the ladder is NOT resume-safe
findings.file_line: src/state/plan_manager.py:122 (self._stuck_state dict); src/state/plan_manager.py:1048-1068 get_stuck_state; escalation_ladder.py:84-122 StuckState docstring 'NOT persisted'
findings.claim: Confirmed exactly. The StuckState (discard_count, pivot_count, search_count, architect_count) lives only in PlanManager._stuck_state, an in-process dict (plan_manager.py:122) that is never written to plan.json or the ledger and never reconstructed on resume. A task that climbed to PIVOT/WEB_SEARCH/SOFT_BLOCKER before a crash/resume restarts the ladder at discard_count=0. This is the OPPOSITE of the resolver's deterministic ladder, whose advancement is resume-safe via _prior_resolution_actions reading the ledger.
findings.evidence: plan_manager.py:118-122: comment says 'v0.15.0: in-memory per-task stuck state for the escalation ladder. Mirrors _in_flight: NOT persisted to plan.json or the ledger; a crash mid-flight resets to defaults.' `self._stuck_state: dict[str, "StuckState"] = {}`. escalation_ladder.py:86-92 docstring: 'held entirely in memory (NOT persisted to plan.json or the ledger)'. plan_manager.py:1070-1098 increment_discard: 'State is in-memory only — no ledger op is appended.' By contrast, the resolver's deterministic ladder advancement IS resume-safe: _prior_resolution_actions (execute_phase.py:1622-1650) reads the on-disk ledger for resolution_chosen ops, so _next_rung advances correctly across restarts. The asymmetry is precisely as claimed: the legacy escalation_ladder counters forget, the resolver's per-class ladder remembers.
findings.repro_or_probe: Unit: pm=PlanManager(tmp); await pm.increment_discard('t') x3; await pm.increment_pivot('t') x3 (drives to SOFT_BLOCKER). Construct FRESH PlanManager(tmp), assert (await pm.get_stuck_state('t')).pivot_count==0 and next_step(stuck_state)=='continue' — proving ladder reset on resume.

The dispatch at 5686 branches solely on `step` (from next_step). repetition_recovery.py:53-61 RecoveryAction Literal is {switch_tactic, increase_scope, decrease_scope, re_architect, kb_lookup, ask_human, do_nothing} — ZERO overlap with StuckStepLabel {continue, REFINE, PIVOT, WEB_SEARCH, ARCHITECT_CONSULT, SOFT_BLOCKER}. findings.title: choose_recovery_action's do_nothing rule is structurally unreachable: qa_gates_passed is read via getattr but is never a Task field and never assigned True anywhere
findings.claim: Confirmed. qa_gates_passed is always False (no Task field, getattr default), so Rule 1 in choose_recovery_action can never fire. The do_nothing RecoveryAction is permanently unreachable. Combined with finding 2 (the whole recovery_action_chosen system is audit-only and never dispatched), this is a doubly-dead path.
findings.evidence: execute_phase.py:5661: `qa_gates_passed = bool(getattr(task, "qa_gates_passed", False))`. repetition_recovery.py:104-110 Rule 1: `if qa_gates_passed and repetition_loop_detected and discard_count >= _LOW_DISCARD_CEILING: return "do_nothing"`. The getattr default is False and no Task field named qa_gates_passed exists in the schemas (confirmed via Task dataclass in state/schemas.py which contains no such field). Even if it could fire, the whole choose_recovery_action result is audit-only (finding 2). This is a double-dead path: structurally unreachable AND not dispatched even if it returned a value.
