findings.title: Resolver is only reachable at the ladder's TWO terminal rungs (soft-blocker, retry-exhaustion); the 4 non-terminal rungs return without ever calling block_task — confirms+localizes the 'precedence-shadowed' seed
findings.file_line: execute_phase.py:5828-5905 soft-blocker→block_task; 5907-5949 pivot returns (no block); 5951-5989 refine returns (no block); 6053-6063 retry-exhaustion→block_task; 6066-6069 retry returns (no block)
findings.claim: Confirmed and localized to file:line. block_task (and thus the resolver chokepoint _maybe_resolve_blocker) is invoked at EXACTLY two sites inside _try_retry_or_escalate: the critic-confirmed soft-blocker rung (5853, failure_class=SOFT_BLOCKER) and the legacy retry-exhaustion rung (6053, failure_class=UNKNOWN). REFINE, PIVOT, WEB_SEARCH, and ARCHITECT_CONSULT all return a re-enabled task WITHOUT calling block_task — the resolver never sees these rungs.
findings.evidence: Traced all branches of _try_retry_or_escalate after `if step != 'continue':` at 5686. ARCHITECT_CONSULT: returns at 5802 (`if arch_resolution is not None: return arch_resolution`) without calling block_task. After critic dispatch, branches: soft-blocker (5828) → calls block_task(SOFT_BLOCKER) at 5853 ✓; pivot (5907) → increments pivot_count + returns at 5949 (no block_task); refine (5951-5989) → updates status to in_progress + returns at 5989 (no block_task). Legacy 'continue' path: new_count >= retry_limit → block_task(UNKNOWN) at 6053 ✓; else retry → returns at 6068 (no block_task). WEB_SEARCH folds into the critic call and the critic decides soft-blocker/pivot/refine. So block_task is called in exactly two places inside this function: soft-blocker (5853) and retry-exhaustion (6053). All non-terminal rungs return without the resolver being consulted.
findings.repro_or_probe: Mark a test resolver_enabled; drive a task to discard_count<3 (REFINE rung); assert _maybe_resolve_blocker is NOT called (spy on it). Then drive pivot_count>=3 and assert _maybe_resolve_blocker IS called once with failure_class SOFT_BLOCKER.

findings.title: Seed correction: the resolver's structural actions are inert ONLY on the DETERMINISTIC path (direction defaults to prose rationale → 0 bullets → 0 tasks); the LLM path can populate params['direction'] and is NOT inert by construction
findings.file_line: execute_phase.py:1763-1765 _apply_resolution direction=params.get('direction') or rationale; corrective_parser.py:79-128 bullet-only parse; blocker_resolver.py:114 _act sets no direction; blocker_resolver.py:601 _parse_resolution model_validate(obj) (params from LLM JSON)
findings.claim: Confirmed with path-specific nuance. Deterministic structural rungs (re_architect, re_plan, narrow_scope, split_task) supply only prose rationale (no 'direction' key in params), so _resolver_corrective always returns None for the deterministic path. The LLM resolver path can return params with a bulleted 'direction' that would parse successfully. The 'inert by construction' characterization applies only to the deterministic fast-path, not universally.
findings.evidence: _act() at blocker_resolver.py:110-114: `def _act(action, rationale, **params) -> ResolutionAction: return ResolutionAction(action=action, params=dict(params), rationale=rationale)`. Deterministic structural rungs (re_architect/re_plan/narrow_scope/split_task) call _act without a direction kwarg — so params={} and the direction in _apply_resolution at 1763-1765 falls back to rationale (prose). execute_phase.py:1763-1765: `direction = str(params.get('direction') or rationale or '')`. corrective_parser.py:79-82 parses ONLY top-level bullets (^[-*]|\d+\.); prose with no bullets returns []. So deterministic structural rungs produce 0 corrective tasks → _resolver_corrective returns None (1713-1714) → fall-through to legacy block. The LLM path (blocker_resolver.py:601 _parse_resolution → model_validate) CAN include params={'direction':'- task1\n- task2'} which WOULD parse to real tasks. Inertness is path-specific.
findings.repro_or_probe: Unit: from orchestrator.blocker_resolver import _act; from orchestrator.corrective_parser import parse_corrective_direction; a=_act('re_architect', 'rethink at component altitude'); assert not a.params.get('direction'); assert parse_corrective_direction(a.rationale, phase_id='1', base_task_count=0)==[].

findings.title: SOFT_BLOCKER terminal rung gets exactly ONE bonus retry from the resolver (consult_knowledge→_resolver_retry re-enable), but the un-decremented in-memory StuckState forces immediate re-escalation → bounded 1-cycle churn
findings.file_line: blocker_resolver.py:315-335 SOFT_BLOCKER ladder consult_knowledge→ask_human; execute_phase.py:1766-1778 _apply_resolution consult_knowledge→_resolver_retry; execute_phase.py:1653-1675 _resolver_retry resets retry_count=0, status→in_progress; escalation_ladder.py:168-172 SOFT_BLOCKER on pivot_count>=3
findings.claim: Confirmed. consult_knowledge (first SOFT_BLOCKER rung) re-enables the task via _resolver_retry. But StuckState.pivot_count is in-memory and still >=3, so the NEXT failure immediately returns SOFT_BLOCKER again; _prior_resolution_actions finds consult_knowledge already tried, so _next_rung returns ask_human → _apply_resolution returns None → real block. The resolver buys exactly one bonus attempt. The two systems (in-memory ladder counters vs ledger-based resolver ladder) are uncoordinated.
findings.evidence: blocker_resolver.py:315-334: SOFT_BLOCKER ladder = [consult_knowledge, ask_human]. _apply_resolution:1766-1778: consult_knowledge → _resolver_retry (re-enables, retry_count=0, status=in_progress). execute_phase.py:5866-5869: 'if updated.status != "blocked": return updated' — skips soft-blocker handoff. BUT escalation_ladder.py:168-172: SOFT_BLOCKER fires when pivot_count >= _PIVOT_SOFT_BLOCKER_THRESHOLD (=3). Since increment_pivot was never called by the resolver (StuckState is in-memory only), the next failure still has pivot_count>=3 → SOFT_BLOCKER again → _prior_resolution_actions reads ledger, finds consult_knowledge was tried → _next_rung advances to ask_human → _apply_resolution returns None (1761) → legacy block. Net: exactly one bonus attempt. The StuckState double-counts.

findings.title: A real re-dispatch is structurally impossible at the phase-degrade site: BlockerContext.task_id is hard-coded None, and BOTH recovery primitives (_resolver_retry, _resolver_corrective) require a non-None Task

findings.title: The phase-degrade resolution_outcome action='observed' diverges from the execute-loop's outcome vocabulary ('recovered'/'ask_human'/'fell_through'), creating a ledger ambiguity that hides the no-op repair
findings.claim: Confirmed exactly as stated: the two ledger vocabularies are disjoint. Phase-degrade writes action='observed'/outcome='phase_degraded'; the execute-loop writes action=<actual ResolutionActionType>/outcome in {recovered, ask_human, fell_through}. 'observed' is not a ResolutionActionType, making it impossible for a ledger query to determine whether the chosen action (repair_environment) was applied or fell through.
findings.evidence: blocker_resolver.py:768-773: writes `{op: 'resolution_outcome', action: 'observed', outcome: 'phase_degraded'}`. execute_phase.py:1890-1896: `act_name = getattr(action, 'action', 'fall_through')` then `outcome = 'recovered' if recovered is not None else 'ask_human' if act_name == 'ask_human' else 'fell_through'` — writes `{action: act_name, outcome: <one of recovered/ask_human/fell_through>}`. Phase-degrade uses `action='observed'` (not a ResolutionActionType member) and `outcome='phase_degraded'` (not in the execute-loop's three-value outcome set). A ledger reader scanning for `outcome in {'fell_through', 'recovered', 'ask_human'}` misses phase-degrade entries. A reader scanning for `action == 'ask_human'` misses that the phase-degrade chose repair_environment before writing 'observed'.

Ledger-consistency test: for every resolution_chosen where action != 'ask_human'/'fall_through' assert an adjacent resolution_outcome with action matching the chosen action — will fail for phase-degrade (action='observed' != 'repair_environment').

findings.title: consult_knowledge action is near-dead: 0.2s timeout + lookup_recent_failures returns '' on no-task/empty/error, so its retry note is almost always the bare rationale
findings.claim: Confirmed. consult_knowledge is the FIRST rung for test_diagnosis_* and soft_blocker ladders. It calls consult_knowledge() bounded at 0.2s; on any miss/timeout/no-task-id it returns '' and the note degrades to `consult_knowledge: {rationale}` (a constant prose string). The note IS written to task metadata as 'resolver_note' via _resolver_retry, but _execute_one never reads resolver_note into last_issues (Finding 2). The 'near-dead' characterization is slightly strong: on a real run with orch.knowledge populated and matching entries within 0.2s, the note CAN be populated — but the developer still doesn't see it (Finding 2 is the binding bug). Severity 'nice' is appropriate: subsumed by Finding 2's fix.
findings.evidence: blocker_resolver.py:71 `_KNOWLEDGE_TIMEOUT_S = 0.2` confirmed. knowledge_lookup.py:51 `_DEFAULT_LOOKUP_TIMEOUT_S: float = 0.1` (the underlying default is even lower). consult_knowledge (lines 399-422): returns '' when task_id is None (409), `orch.knowledge` is None (100 in knowledge_lookup), store times out (asyncio.TimeoutError at 0.2s), or no matching entries. execute_phase.py:1773-1777: when summary is empty, `note = f'consult_knowledge: {rationale}'` — the constant prose rationale. Then `_resolver_retry(orch, task, note=note)` at line 1778 writes this to metadata['resolver_note'] but (per Finding 2) this note is never read by the developer. Compound effect: the consult_knowledge rung's net effect is a bare retry with a 0.2s KB read whose note is (a) high-probability empty/timeout and (b) discarded from the developer's input regardless of KB read success.
findings.repro_or_probe: grep -n '_KNOWLEDGE_TIMEOUT_S' src/orchestrator/blocker_resolver.py → line 71: 0.2. Field probe: enable resolver, trigger test_diagnosis_hardfail twice; inspect resolution_chosen note in ledger — confirm it is 'consult_knowledge: test diagnosis is terminal...' (the constant prose fallback) rather than real prior-failure summaries. Fix = raise the timeout AND wire the summary into last_issues (subsumed by Finding 2's fix: read meta['resolver_note'] into last_issues at the top of _execute_one when resolver_action=='retry').

findings.title: Empty/max-tokens reviewer (subtype=None) is misrouted to the developer-charging genuine-MALFORMED path, not the infra soft-pass path — the A1 fix only catches the literal error_max_turns subtype
findings.file_line: src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py:4711-4712 (_reviewer_exhausted_turns check); execute_phase.py:7118-7120 (_TURN_EXHAUSTION_SUBTYPES); execute_phase.py:4822-4839 (genuine-MALFORMED → _try_retry_or_escalate); src/adapters/claude_code.py:491-519 (empty result, subtype=None when no api_error_status)
findings.claim: The A1 fix at execute_phase.py:4711-4712 gates exclusively on subtype in _TURN_EXHAUSTION_SUBTYPES = {'error_max_turns', 'error_max_turns_escalation_exhausted'}. A reviewer that produces an empty body due to output-token cap (not a turn-count cap) returns AgentResult(success=False, text='', subtype=None) per claude_code.py:491-519. subtype=None is not in the frozenset, so _reviewer_exhausted_turns returns False, and the MALFORMED falls straight to the developer-discard path at 4822, re-dispatching the developer and burning retry budget — exactly the Run-3 failure mode A1 was supposed to fix. The fix is complete only for the literal error_max_turns signal.
findings.evidence: I traced the path directly: (1) claude_code.py:491-519 documents 'A genuine empty result (no status) keeps subtype=None so the hard-fail behaviour is preserved.' (2) _TURN_EXHAUSTION_SUBTYPES at execute_phase.py:7118-7120 is frozenset({'error_max_turns','error_max_turns_escalation_exhausted'}). (3) _reviewer_exhausted_turns at 7143-7144 does: `return review_result.subtype in _TURN_EXHAUSTION_SUBTYPES` — python confirms `None in frozenset(...)` == False. (4) execute_phase.py:4711 check is NOT entered when subtype=None, so control falls to 4822 `if verdict == 'MALFORMED':` → _try_retry_or_escalate(..., reason='reviewer MALFORMED'). (5) The only reviewer infra tests (test_orchestrator_execute_phase_reviewer_infra.py) all stub `subtype='error_max_turns'`; no test uses subtype=None. Finding fully confirmed.
findings.repro_or_probe: Add a test mirroring test_orchestrator_execute_phase_reviewer_infra.py::test_reviewer_exhaustion_retries_then_soft_passes but stub the reviewer to return AgentResult(success=False, text='', subtype=None). Assert the developer is re-dispatched (adapter.count('developer')==2) and retry_count increments — confirming the misroute. The fix should add output-cap detection (empty text + no error_max_turns but no api_error_status either) to the infra disambiguation.

findings.title: Reviewer budget-escalation ladder NEVER fires for the dominant empty-reviewer MALFORMED case — subtype=None resets the (task,reviewer) counter on every call
findings.file_line: src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py:6653-6654 (delegate calls record_result after every dispatch); src/orchestrator/budget_escalation.py:239-253 (record_result: only 'error_max_turns' increments, everything else pops/clears)
findings.claim: BudgetEscalationTracker.record_result at budget_escalation.py:249-253 increments only on subtype=='error_max_turns' and CLEARS the counter on all other subtypes including None. Since an empty reviewer response returns subtype=None (per Finding 1 above), each such call resets the counter to 0. The per-(task_id,'reviewer') escalation counter thus never advances and max_turns is never bumped for the empty-reviewer failure mode. This compounds Finding 1: not only does the misroute re-dispatch the developer, but it does so with no reviewer turn-budget escalation on the re-runs.
findings.evidence: I read budget_escalation.py:239-253 directly. record_result(scope_id, role, subtype): 'if subtype == "error_max_turns": self._counters[key] = self._counters.get(key,0)+1 else: self._counters.pop(key, None)'. Any non-'error_max_turns' subtype (including None) clears the counter. execute_phase.py:6653-6654 calls _budget_tracker.record_result(envelope.task_id, role, result.subtype) after every delegate return. So a reviewer returning AgentResult(subtype=None) resets counter to 0 on every call — the escalation ladder never advances for the empty-result case and the reviewer is re-dispatched at base max_turns each loop iteration. The module docstring explicitly states 'Escalation ONLY fires for error_max_turns' (budget_escalation.py line 21).
findings.repro_or_probe: Unit test against BudgetEscalationTracker: tracker.record_result('t','reviewer',None) called 3 times, then assert tracker.current_attempt('t','reviewer')==0. Field probe: in a run with repeated empty reviewer responses, grep .autodev ledger for op='budget_escalation' with role='reviewer' — expect ZERO such ops regardless of how many times the reviewer fails empty.

findings.title: No dedicated MALFORMED counter: reviewer-machinery failures share the developer's qa_retry_limit/discard budget — a reviewer infra glitch consumes the developer's content-retry quota
findings.claim: There is no dedicated MALFORMED retry counter in _execute_one. Both the genuine-MALFORMED path (4833) and NEEDS_CHANGES/REJECTED (4847) call the same _try_retry_or_escalate, which increments the shared discard_count and mark_task_retry. A reviewer machinery failure (MALFORMED from infra, or genuine parse failure) steals directly from the developer's content-revision budget. A task with qa_retry_limit=3 that suffers 1 MALFORMED + 2 NEEDS_CHANGES escalates after the 3rd combined _try_retry_or_escalate call with no way to distinguish the cause.
findings.evidence: I read execute_phase.py:4822-4853 directly. The MALFORMED branch (4833) and the NEEDS_CHANGES/REJECTED branch (4847) both call the identical `_try_retry_or_escalate(orch, task, retry_limit, reason=...)`. Both routes converge on the same increment_discard (5591 via _try_retry_or_escalate→plan_manager.increment_discard) and mark_task_retry (5992). Grep for any dedicated MALFORMED counter: `grep -rn 'malformed_count' src/` returns no results. The only per-kind local in _execute_one scope is `test_diag_attempts` (for test diagnosis, line 4325) — no equivalent for MALFORMED. All MALFORMED retries share the same `qa_retry_limit` bucket as genuine NEEDS_CHANGES retries.
findings.repro_or_probe: Test: stub reviewer = [AgentResult(success=True, text='prose no verdict', subtype=None), 'NEEDS_CHANGES', 'NEEDS_CHANGES', ...] with qa_retry_limit=3. Assert the task escalates after the 3rd combined _try_retry_or_escalate and that discard_count/retry_count does not distinguish the first MALFORMED from the two NEEDS_CHANGES. Inspect ledger recovery_action_chosen ops for interleaved reason strings ('reviewer MALFORMED' then 'reviewer NEEDS_CHANGES') against a single rising discard_count.

findings.title: Retry-state divergence across resume: persisted retry_count keeps climbing while in-memory StuckState.discard_count (the ladder input) and the budget tracker both reset to 0 — the ladder/resolver restarts under a task that is already near escalation
findings.file_line: src/state/plan_manager.py:114-122 (_stuck_state: NOT persisted); src/orchestrator/budget_escalation.py:33-35 (NOT persisted across resume); src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py:4194 (unconditional update_task_status in_progress)
findings.claim: The three retry signals diverge across a resume boundary. task.retry_count IS persisted (mark_task_retry → plan.json/ledger at plan_manager.py:1221-1235). _stuck_state.discard_count is NOT persisted (plan_manager.py:114-122 comment: 'NOT persisted to plan.json or the ledger'). BudgetEscalationTracker._counters is NOT persisted (budget_escalation.py:33-35 comment: 'NOT persisted across resume, by design'). execute_phase.py:4194 unconditionally re-enters in_progress with no skip for a task that was mid-MALFORMED-loop before crash. On resume, a task with retry_count=2 (one slot left) restarts the ladder at discard_count=0, potentially getting 3 more discard attempts before the ladder advances — making escalation non-deterministic across resume for MALFORMED loops.
findings.evidence: I read plan_manager.py:114-122 directly: 'v0.15.0: in-memory per-task stuck state for the escalation ladder. Mirrors _in_flight: NOT persisted to plan.json or the ledger; a crash mid-flight resets to defaults.' The _stuck_state dict is initialized empty in __init__ (line 122). I read budget_escalation.py:33-35: 'in-memory only — NOT persisted across resume, by design — repeated max-turns in a fresh session starts the escalation ladder over.' I read execute_phase.py:4194: task = await orch.plan_manager.update_task_status(task.id, 'in_progress') — unconditional, no resume-state check before the while loop. By contrast, mark_task_retry at plan_manager.py:1221-1235 persists retry_count via ledger_append + snapshot_plan. So after resume: retry_count may be 2 (near qa_retry_limit), but discard_count=0 and budget_escalation_counter=0 — the ladder rediscovers the task has a history only after it fails again.
findings.repro_or_probe: Test: drive a task to discard_count=2 via two MALFORMED retries (via _try_retry_or_escalate), then construct a fresh Orchestrator over the same plan.json (simulating resume) and call _execute_one again. Assert (await plan_manager.get_stuck_state(task.id)).discard_count==0 while task.retry_count==2 — proving the divergence. Field probe: in a resumed run, plan.json carries retry_count>0 but there is no persisted discard_count in .autodev/state/ (confirmed by absence of any 'increment_discard' ledger op — that function explicitly appends no ledger op per plan_manager.py:1074).

findings.title: Tournament-path reviewer MALFORMED disambiguates on orch._last_adapter_subtype, a single mutable global last-write — multi-candidate/post-tournament dispatches can make the last subtype unrepresentative of the winning verdict's reviewer
findings.file_line: src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py:4577 (review_result=None for tournament path); execute_phase.py:4711-4712 (_reviewer_exhausted_turns(orch, review_result) where review_result=None); execute_phase.py:7143-7146 (_reviewer_exhausted_turns fallback to orch._last_adapter_subtype); execute_phase.py:6644 (orch._last_adapter_subtype overwritten on every delegate call)
findings.claim: On the review-tournament path, review_result stays None and _reviewer_exhausted_turns falls back to orch._last_adapter_subtype (execute_phase.py:7145), which is overwritten by every delegate call in the tournament runner (line 6644). Because the tournament dispatches candidate A plus multiple judge roles (all via delegate), _last_adapter_subtype after the tournament reflects the last judge dispatch — not the winning candidate's actual subtype. A tournament where candidate A produced a genuine bad-diff MALFORMED but the last judge exhausted turns would incorrectly soft-pass the bad diff. The ReviewCandidate schema has no subtype field, so there is no mechanism to recover the per-candidate subtype after the tournament returns.
findings.evidence: I traced the full tournament path: (1) execute_phase.py:4577 initializes review_result=None and does NOT assign it in the tournament branch (4581-4651 — the tournament branch only sets verdict/issues from review_tournament_outcome). (2) At 4711, _reviewer_exhausted_turns(orch, None) is called, which at 7143 takes the `review_result is not None` branch to False, then 7145-7146 falls back to `orch._last_adapter_subtype`. (3) _last_adapter_subtype is set at 6644 after EVERY delegate call. The tournament runner (review_tournament_runner.py:588-625) dispatches at minimum 3 candidates per round (A via _build_candidate_a→delegate, B via _call_role_with_prompt, AB via _call_role_with_prompt) plus N judges via _run_judge_cohort (each judge calls delegate). (4) ReviewCandidate (schemas.py:806-844) has no subtype field — the per-candidate adapter subtype is not preserved anywhere after the tournament. (5) The code comment at 4575-4576 acknowledges the fallback: 'the tournament path falls back to orch._last_adapter_subtype'. The last-write-wins design is intentional but the hazard is real: if candidate A (the winning MALFORMED) was dispatched early and a later judge happened to exhaust turns (error_max_turns), the disambiguation wrongly treats A's genuine bad-diff MALFORMED as infra and soft-passes it.
findings.repro_or_probe: Enable cfg.tournaments.review_tournament_enabled and stub a tournament whose WINNING candidate A is a genuine (non-exhaustion) MALFORMED reviewer response but whose last judge dispatch returns AgentResult(subtype='error_max_turns'). Assert the code calls the soft-pass path (wrong) because _last_adapter_subtype=='error_max_turns' by the time _reviewer_exhausted_turns(orch,None) is evaluated. Fix: add a subtype field to ReviewCandidate and propagate the candidate A adapter subtype through ReviewTournamentResult so execute_phase can read the winner's actual subtype rather than the last-write global.

findings.title: qa_gates_passed recovery signal is permanently dead: Task has no such attribute, getattr default False always wins, so the do_nothing convergence rule can never fire and the infra soft-pass never reaches it
findings.claim: Confirmed verbatim: execute_phase.py:5661 uses `bool(getattr(task, 'qa_gates_passed', False))` against a Task model that has NO qa_gates_passed field (Task defined at schemas.py:163-304, all fields enumerated). The getattr always returns False. repetition_recovery.py:105-110 Rule 1 requires qa_gates_passed=True AND repetition_loop_detected AND discard>=2 to return 'do_nothing'. Since qa_gates_passed is permanently False, 'do_nothing' is statically unreachable. Additionally, choose_recovery_action is itself audit-only (execute_phase.py:5655-5660 admits it), so even if 'do_nothing' could fire, it would not route anywhere.
findings.evidence: 1) python3 probe: `from state.schemas import Task; t = Task(id='1.1', phase_id='1', title='t', description='d'); print(hasattr(t, 'qa_gates_passed'))` → False; `getattr(t, 'qa_gates_passed', 'MISSING')` → 'MISSING'. 2) grep confirms zero `qa_gates_passed =` write sites on Task objects in src/. 3) execute_phase.py:5661 reads `bool(getattr(task, 'qa_gates_passed', False))` — always False. 4) choose_recovery_action probe: with qa_gates_passed=False + repetition_loop_detected=True + discard_count=2 → returns 'switch_tactic' (not 'do_nothing'); with qa_gates_passed=True → returns 'do_nothing'. 5) ReviewEvidence.model_fields shows ['task_id','kind','verdict','issues','output_text','raw_response'] — no soft_passed field that could feed the qa_gates signal even indirectly. 6) repetition_recovery.py:104-110 Rule 1 requires qa_gates_passed==True to return 'do_nothing'; this branch is statically dead in the field.
findings.repro_or_probe: python3 -c "import sys; sys.path.insert(0,'src'); from state.schemas import Task; t=Task(id='1.1',phase_id='1',title='t',description='d'); print(getattr(t,'qa_gates_passed','MISSING'))" → 'MISSING'. Then: from orchestrator.repetition_recovery import choose_recovery_action; assert choose_recovery_action(2,0,0,False,True)=='switch_tactic' (never 'do_nothing'). Severity lowered from 'should' to 'should' — the do_nothing branch is already an audit-only annotation (per finding about choose_recovery_action being inert) so the double-dead is confirmed but the severity is no worse than the parent.

findings.title: Infra reviewer soft-pass writes a ReviewEvidence schema-identical to a genuine APPROVED; the only differentiator is a free-text issues[0] marker that NO production consumer reads
findings.claim: Confirmed verbatim: ReviewEvidence (schemas.py:490-506) has no soft_passed/soft_pass_reason field — those fields exist only on TestEvidence (schemas.py:554-555). The infra soft-pass at execute_phase.py:4802-4816 stamps ReviewEvidence(verdict='APPROVED', issues=['reviewer_infra_softpass: ...']). The marker string appears in exactly two src/ locations (both write sites). Zero machine consumers in src/ check for the 'reviewer_infra_softpass' key in issues. The only src/ readers of .issues are in review_tournament_runner.py and are pure prose-formatting/equality, not branching on the infra marker. A genuine APPROVED and an infra soft-pass APPROVED are byte-for-byte indistinguishable to every downstream machine consumer.
findings.evidence: 1) schemas.py:490-506: ReviewEvidence fields are ['task_id','kind','verdict','issues','output_text','raw_response'] — no soft_passed or soft_pass_reason field. TestEvidence at schemas.py:554-555 has soft_passed/soft_pass_reason; ReviewEvidence does not. 2) execute_phase.py:4802-4816: infra soft-pass writes ReviewEvidence(verdict='APPROVED', issues=['reviewer_infra_softpass: ...']). 3) python3 probe: ReviewEvidence(task_id='1.1',verdict='APPROVED',issues=[]).model_fields == ReviewEvidence(task_id='1.1',verdict='APPROVED',issues=['reviewer_infra_softpass: ...']).model_fields — both have identical field sets; verdict=='APPROVED' in both cases. 4) grep -rn 'reviewer_infra_softpass' src/ → ONLY execute_phase.py:4793 (logger call) and :4804 (issues string write). 5) review_tournament_runner.py reads .issues only for prose formatting (lines 246,294,301,362-363) and for an equality check (line 485 set(x.issues)==set(y.issues)) — none branches on the infra marker substring. 6) tests/test_orchestrator_execute_phase_reviewer_infra.py:178-180 only asserts the marker IS present in issues, never that any decision branches on it.
findings.repro_or_probe: python3 -c "import sys;sys.path.insert(0,'src');from state.schemas import ReviewEvidence; genuine=ReviewEvidence(task_id='1.1',verdict='APPROVED',issues=[],output_text='ok',raw_response='VERDICT: APPROVED'); sp=ReviewEvidence(task_id='1.1',verdict='APPROVED',issues=['reviewer_infra_softpass: exhausted turns'],output_text='',raw_response=None); print('gate indistinguishable:', genuine.verdict==sp.verdict=='APPROVED')" → True. Fix: add soft_passed:bool|None=None + soft_pass_reason:str|None=None to ReviewEvidence mirroring TestEvidence, and set soft_passed=True at execute_phase.py:4809.

findings.title: Resume-path completion gate _maybe_accept_approved_on_exhaustion reads only verdict==APPROVED and ignores the soft-pass marker, so an infra-soft-passed review can later auto-complete a turn-exhausted task as genuinely certified
findings.claim: Confirmed verbatim: _maybe_accept_approved_on_exhaustion (execute_phase.py:7149-7280) reads persisted review evidence and gates on verdict!='APPROVED' (line 7209) and empty in-hand diff (line 7218). It never inspects issues[] or any soft_passed field. Since the infra soft-pass writes verdict='APPROVED' (line 4802/4811) — indistinguishable from a genuine APPROVED per Finding 2 — a subsequent developer turn-exhaustion with an empty diff will cause the function to auto-complete the task at line 7262-7266, promoting an un-reviewer-verified diff to a fully certified completion. The scenario requires a subsequent developer turn-exhaustion with empty diff, which is a real field pattern.
findings.evidence: 1) execute_phase.py:7149-7266: _maybe_accept_approved_on_exhaustion re-reads review evidence via `read_evidence(orch.cwd, task.id, 'review')` at line 7199 and gates solely on `getattr(review_ev, 'verdict', None) != 'APPROVED'` at line 7209, plus empty in-hand diff at line 7218. 2) There is no inspection of `review_ev.issues` anywhere in the function (lines 7149-7280 scanned). 3) The function checks `subtype not in _TURN_EXHAUSTION_SUBTYPES` (line 7193) for the DEVELOPER result's subtype — not for a reviewer taint. 4) An infra-soft-pass ReviewEvidence has verdict='APPROVED' (execute_phase.py:4802,4811), so lines 7199-7210 pass the gate. 5) On success, line 7262-7266 walks the task to 'complete' with evidence_bundle pointing at the soft-passed review file. 6) _TURN_EXHAUSTION_SUBTYPES at line 7118-7120 contains only {'error_max_turns','error_max_turns_escalation_exhausted'} — not any soft-pass marker.
findings.repro_or_probe: Test: (1) write a ReviewEvidence with verdict=APPROVED and issues=['reviewer_infra_softpass: ...'] to {task_id}-review.json; (2) construct an AgentResult with subtype='error_max_turns' and diff=None; (3) call _maybe_accept_approved_on_exhaustion(orch, task, developer_result); (4) assert it returns a completed task (NOT None) — demonstrating the soft-pass auto-completes as a genuine certification. Fix: check `review_ev.issues` for the infra marker string, OR add `soft_passed:bool|None=None` to ReviewEvidence and gate on `not review_ev.soft_passed` at line 7209.

findings.title: Soft-passed APPROVED verdict flows through the live test step into the impl tournament and completion carrying tests_passed=passed, with no soft-pass taint on the propagated QA signal
findings.claim: Confirmed: after the infra soft-pass stamps verdict='APPROVED' at line 4802, control proceeds to 'reviewed' status and Step 5 (test_engineer) at line 4856 with no branch on the soft-pass. ImplBundle (impl_tournament.py:55-72) has no soft-pass field. tests_passed=passed in the bundle (execute_phase.py:5283) comes from the test step, not the review. The completed task carries no machine-readable flag distinguishing a soft-passed from a genuine review. Combined with zero-test repos (TestEvidence.soft_passed covers only the test soft-pass, not the review soft-pass), a task can complete with neither a genuine reviewer verdict NOR a genuine test signal and nothing in its state or evidence flags either condition.
findings.evidence: 1) execute_phase.py:4802 sets verdict='APPROVED' in the infra soft-pass branch; control falls through to line 4854 (update_task_status 'reviewed') with no early return or continue. 2) Step 5 (test_engineer dispatch at line 4856+) runs unconditionally after the reviewed status update — the soft-pass taint is not checked here. 3) ImplBundle at impl_tournament.py:55-72: fields are [task_id, task_description, diff, files_changed, tests_passed, tests_failed, tests_total, test_output_excerpt, variant_label, notes] — no review_soft_passed or infra_taint field. 4) execute_phase.py:5283 builds ImplBundle(tests_passed=passed, ...) where 'passed' comes from the test step result, not the review — the soft-pass review does not affect this value. 5) grep -rn 'soft_pass' src/tournament/impl_tournament.py → 0 results. 6) The task metadata.get('reviewer_infra_softpass') is never set anywhere — only 'resolver_note' and 'dynamic_scope_expansion_used' are written to task.metadata in this path. So no flag reaches the completed Task state.
findings.repro_or_probe: Field probe: force a reviewer to exhaust turns (small turn budget) against a repo with no discoverable tests; assert the task reaches status='complete' and its review evidence has verdict=APPROVED with an infra marker in issues but no soft_passed field on ReviewEvidence; assert ImplBundle.tests_passed=0 with no review_soft_passed. Confirms downstream treats infra soft-pass as genuine green end-to-end. Fix: (a) add soft_passed to ReviewEvidence and propagate it into ImplBundle, (b) gate the completion path on soft_passed=False.

findings.title: Sparse-checkout repair is Python/POSIX-only by construction — detect_missing_paths parses ZERO paths from Go/Rust/TS/JS/Java missing-module errors → repair is INERT for every non-Python first-class language
findings.claim: Confirmed exactly as stated. _MISSING_FILE_PATTERNS's three regexes cover only Python FileNotFoundError, generic 'cannot open' quoted-path, and POSIX '<token>: No such file or directory'. Go 'cannot find package', TS 'Cannot find module', Rust 'unresolved import', Java 'cannot find symbol' all return []. Since sparse-checkout is the default for huge repos (execute_phase.py:4221-4224 reads cfg.worktree_sparse_checkout_enabled), a Go/Rust/TS/Java task that sparse-misses a needed path gets zero expansion — it falls straight to the retry ladder with an unchanged worktree where the same miss recurs.
findings.evidence: I read worktree.py:1013-1057 directly. The three regexes in _MISSING_FILE_PATTERNS are: (1) `No such file or directory:\s*['"]([^'"\n]+)['"]` (Python FileNotFoundError quoted path); (2) `cannot open\s+['"]([^'"\n]+)['"]` (generic quoted form); (3) `(?:^|\s)([^\s:'"]+):\s*No such file or directory` (POSIX token-colon-NoSuchFile). I ran detect_missing_paths live against Go ('cannot find package "foo/bar" in any of:'), TS ('error TS2307: Cannot find module'), Rust ('error[E0432]: unresolved import'), and Java ('error: cannot find symbol') — all returned []. Only the Python FileNotFoundError returned ['src/qa/util.py']. The code at execute_phase.py:5422-5424 short-circuits with `return False` when detect_missing_paths returns [], so no expansion fires for non-Python languages.
findings.repro_or_probe: python3 -c "import sys; sys.path.insert(0,'src'); from orchestrator.worktree import detect_missing_paths; print(detect_missing_paths('cannot find package \"foo/bar\" in any of:')); print(detect_missing_paths(\"error TS2307: Cannot find module './foo'\"))" — both print []. Confirmed by live run: Go/TS/Rust/Java all return [].

findings.title: _maybe_expand_sparse_for_missing returns True even when git refused the widen (rc!=0) — the True return is NOT evidence the worktree changed, so it burns a free retry that fixed nothing
findings.file_line: src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py:5457-5483 (try/except only catches exceptions); src/orchestrator/worktree.py:690-712 (expand_sparse_paths swallows rc!=0 and returns None)
findings.claim: Confirmed. `expand_sparse_paths` silently no-ops on git rc!=0 (returns None, never raises). `_maybe_expand_sparse_for_missing` has no mechanism to distinguish a successful expansion from a silent git failure — both produce no exception, both cause `return True`. On a non-sparse worktree `git sparse-checkout add` returns rc=128 ('fatal: no sparse-checkout to add to'), which is swallowed, yet the helper reports True, flags `dynamic_scope_expansion_used=True`, and re-dispatches the developer against an unchanged worktree. The only False paths are: no missing paths detected, no scope, no paths in-scope, or expand_sparse_paths raises WorktreeError (only when worktree directory does not exist, line 679).

findings.title: The one-shot guard flag is in-memory only and never persisted — lost on the next update_task_status reload and across process resume
findings.file_line: src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py:4454 (read), 4469 (write), 4533 (task reassigned by update_task_status('coded')); src/state/plan_manager.py:345 (_find_task reloads task from disk, flag absent)
findings.claim: Confirmed with precision. `dynamic_scope_expansion_used` is effective ONLY within a single uninterrupted failure-retry sub-loop (before any `update_task_status` call returns a new Task object). It IS correctly guarded for the immediate expand→retry sequence (the `continue` keeps the same in-memory task object). But it is lost after (a) any `update_task_status` that reassigns the `task` variable (e.g., 'coded' at 4533 after developer succeeds post-expansion), (b) process resume (new Orchestrator → _load_sync from disk). Consequence A: within a single run, if QA-gate/reviewer fails after expansion and `_try_retry_or_escalate` eventually re-runs the developer, the flag is gone (task was reloaded) and a second expansion can fire for a different missing file. Consequence B: on resume, the 'one-shot' protection is silently reset.
findings.evidence: I read execute_phase.py:4467-4473 (flag write + continue), and plan_manager.py:320-428 (update_task_status). `update_task_status` at line 339-428 does `async with plan_lock`: `plan = self._load_sync()` (line 340, reads from disk), then `task = _find_task(plan, task_id)` (line 345, returns the on-disk task), modifies `task.status` and known meta fields only, then `snapshot_plan` + returns the freshly-loaded task. The `dynamic_scope_expansion_used` key set at line 4469 is NOT in the `meta=` parameter nor in the known-keys list (blocked_reason, retry_count, last_retry_at, escalated, evidence_bundle, block_reason_class, recovery_hint at lines 379-418). So `update_task_status` at execute_phase.py:4533 returns a Task object loaded from disk without the flag. Any subsequent developer failure would pass the guard at line 4454 (`not task.metadata.get('dynamic_scope_expansion_used')` == True) and fire a second expansion. Across resume: `_load_sync` reads the on-disk snapshot which never had the flag serialized, so the guard is always False after restart.
findings.repro_or_probe: Test: run an expansion (flag set in-memory), then call `update_task_status(task.id,'coded')` and inspect `returned_task.metadata.get('dynamic_scope_expansion_used')` — confirms absent. Then assert a second forced missing-file failure on the returned task would pass the guard at line 4454 and enter expansion again (second expansion fires). For resume: construct two PlanManagers over the same cwd and assert the second sees empty task.metadata.

findings.title: Per-task backoff budget hard-halt (test_diag_budget_exhausted → InfrastructureCircuitOpenError) is mathematically unreachable under every production config
findings.claim: cumulative_backoff_s is a per-task function-scope local (execute_phase.py:4332) that resets on every _execute_one invocation. The per-task retry ladder caps each diagnosis at exactly 2 attempts (attempt 1 → continue, attempt 2 → soft-pass or hard-fail+return). Even with the exponent saturated at max (both sleeps capped at 120s), max per-task cumulative is 2 × 120 = 240s, strictly below the 600s default budget and any budget > 240s. The InfrastructureCircuitOpenError raise at line 5057 is dead code under every default production config.
findings.evidence: Per-task retry ladder exits after exactly 2 attempts: attempt 1 → `elif attempts==1: continue` (line 5155→5181); attempt 2 → soft-pass (capture_failed, line 5110-5153) or hard-fail+return (collection_failed/runtime_crash, line 5182-5230). cumulative_backoff_s is function-scope (line 4332), so max accumulation per task is 2 × backoff_max_s = 2 × 120 = 240s. Default test_diag_backoff_total_budget_s = 600 (schema.py:1497). Probe: driving a breaker with high exponent (20 prior events to saturate cap), then 2 task attempts yields cumulative=240s vs budget=600 → tripped=False. The raise at line 5057 is dead code under every config where budget > 240s.

findings.title: Shared breaker exponent + per-task cumulative reset injects up to 200s of pure wasted real-time sleep into tasks that are predetermined to soft-pass
findings.claim: _test_diag_failure_count_at_threshold (the exponent n) lives on the single shared orch._circuit_breaker (orchestrator/__init__.py:225) and increments monotonically across ALL tasks. cumulative_backoff_s resets per task (execute_phase.py:4332). So later tasks that cross the (cross-task) threshold get a HIGH exponent backoff (80s, 120s) and actually sleep it at line 5072 — even though they will soft-pass at attempt 2. The actual maximum per-task sleep is 2 × backoff_max_s = 240s (not 200s as stated). The sleep is real wall-clock with no functional benefit since the task soft-passes anyway.
findings.evidence: _test_diag_failure_count_at_threshold is on the shared orch._circuit_breaker instance (circuit_breaker.py:187, 427) and increments on every next_backoff_s_for_test_diag() call across all tasks/workers — never reset per-task. cumulative_backoff_s is function-scope (execute_phase.py:4332), reset per _execute_one. Probe: after 3 cross-task events (n=1 exponent), task 2 gets backoffs of 10s + 20s = 30s cumulative vs budget 600s (not tripped). With high exponent (n=5+), both sleeps cap at 120s → 240s per task of real wall-clock sleep. Finding slightly underestimates: actual maximum is 240s (2 × 120s), not 200s. Core claim confirmed: cross-task exponent growth causes later tasks to sleep large amounts even though they are predetermined to soft-pass at attempt 2.

findings.title: Backoff sleep does not relieve the rate-limit pressure it was built for: the sleeping worker idles while sibling parallel workers keep hammering the API; on a sibling halt the sleeping task is cancelled with NO recovery decision
findings.file_line: src/orchestrator/execute_phase.py:5072 (per-worker asyncio.sleep) + :3012-3030 (dispatcher cancels in-flight workers on InfrastructureCircuitOpenError)
findings.claim: The backoff sleep at line 5072 idles only the single worker — all sibling parallel workers continue dispatching to the API, providing zero rate-limit relief. When any sibling raises InfrastructureCircuitOpenError, the dispatcher at 3012-3015 cancels in-flight workers including those mid-asyncio.sleep. The sleeping task receives CancelledError (absorbed by gather at 3028-3030) and is left in `reviewed` status (not `in_progress` as the finding states — the last update_task_status is line 4854 `reviewed`), with no block_task/recovery ledger op. The finding's mention of `in_progress` as the abandoned state is a minor error; `reviewed` is correct.
findings.evidence: asyncio.sleep(backoff_s) at line 5072 runs inside the per-worker coroutine. The dispatcher at lines 3012-3015 calls `other.cancel()` for all in-flight workers when one raises InfrastructureCircuitOpenError (caught at line 2990). asyncio.CancelledError is a BaseException (Python 3.8+), not caught by any `except Exception` in _execute_one. It propagates through the while True loop and the task wrapper. The dispatcher's `asyncio.gather(*_pending_drain, return_exceptions=True)` at lines 3028-3030 absorbs it. At the time of sleep (line 5072), the task's last update_task_status was `reviewed` (line 4854) — the task is left in `reviewed` state with no block_task or recovery op. The core architectural claim is confirmed: one sleeping worker does not reduce concurrency for the remaining workers.
findings.repro_or_probe: Field probe: run with parallel workers + soft-pass disabled + tiny budget so one worker trips budget (InfrastructureCircuitOpenError at line 5057) while another is in asyncio.sleep at 5072; after the halt, inspect the second task's status in the plan — expect `reviewed` (not `blocked`) with no `blocker_escalated`/`resolution_chosen` op in the ledger for it.

findings.title: is_bug_fix() substring-matches bug markers → feature/refactor/docs specs wrongly enter diagnosis (leaky skip gate)

findings.title: block_hook registration swallowed — resolver silently disabled for the entire run
findings.claim: The `setattr` silent swallow (lines 2249-2253) is confirmed, but the resolver is NOT fully disabled: `blocker_guard._resolve()` has a functional call-time import fallback (`from orchestrator.execute_phase import _maybe_resolve_blocker`) that fires whenever `orch.block_hook` is absent. The claim about 'resolver inert' on registration failure overstates the consequence; the correct finding is registration failure causes every `block_task` call to pay a repeated import, and the `block_hook` fast-path is never used.
findings.evidence: Lines 2249-2253 confirm the `try: setattr(...) except Exception: pass` pattern. However, `blocker_guard._resolve()` at lines 55-59 of `blocker_guard.py` has a call-time fallback: `if hook is None: from orchestrator.execute_phase import _maybe_resolve_blocker; hook = _maybe_resolve_blocker`. This import is cycle-safe at runtime (per the module docstring at line 53). The finder's claim that a circular import would leave `hook` as `None` and the resolver inert is not confirmed — the call-time import path is functional. The real risk is narrower: if `setattr` fails silently, every `block_task` call pays the import overhead on each invocation, and if `execute_phase` is not yet in `sys.modules` at block time the import would attempt a fresh load, but by any block time the module is always fully loaded.

findings.title: `_maybe_resolve_blocker` inner except BLE001 at :1842 resets counts to `{}` on setattr failure — cycle guard uses ephemeral dict
findings.claim: Claim confirmed exactly. The inner except at 1842-1843 creates a NEW empty dict that replaces the one that was being tracked, and this ephemeral dict is never stored to orch. This is distinct from finding #1 (outer except): even when the outer try succeeds, this inner setattr failure renders the cycle guard permanently ineffective for orchestrators that prevent dynamic attribute setting.
findings.evidence: Lines 1838-1846 confirm exactly: `counts = getattr(orch, '_resolver_cycle_counts', None); if counts is None: counts = {}; try: orch._resolver_cycle_counts = counts except Exception: counts = {}; if counts.get(guard_key, 0) >= max_cycles: return None; counts[guard_key] = counts.get(guard_key, 0) + 1`. When `setattr` raises at line 1841, the `except Exception` at 1842 reassigns `counts = {}` (a new empty dict, distinct from the one attempted to be stored). The increment at 1846 modifies this ephemeral dict. On the next call, `getattr(orch, '_resolver_cycle_counts', None)` still returns `None` (since the setattr always fails), so a fresh `{}` is created again, and the guard check at 1844 always sees count 0. The per-blocker budget is never exhausted.
findings.repro_or_probe: Create an orchestrator with `__setattr__` raising `AttributeError` for `_resolver_cycle_counts`; call `_maybe_resolve_blocker` 10 times with the same (task_id, failure_class); each call sees `counts = {}` (ephemeral), increments to `{key: 1}`, but `orch` still has no `_resolver_cycle_counts`; the guard never fires and the LLM is called on every iteration.

findings.title: [] → --allowed-tools "" does NOT disable tools; correct flag is --tools ""
findings.claim: When inv.allowed_tools==[], the adapter emits --allowed-tools "" to the Claude CLI. The Claude CLI IGNORES an empty string to --allowed-tools and grants all tools. The correct flag to disable all built-in tools is --tools "". This is a live-confirmed causal link to the A4 regression (critic_t burns turns on file reads).
findings.evidence: Live CLI probe on claude v2.1.177 (installed at /opt/homebrew/bin/claude): `claude -p "Run bash: echo BASH_RAN" --allowed-tools "" --max-turns 2 --output-format json` returned result='Done — output was BASH_RAN.' (stop_reason=end_turn, is_error=false) — Bash executed despite the empty --allowed-tools. In contrast, `claude -p "Run bash: echo BASH_RAN" --tools "" --max-turns 2 --output-format json` returned result='I can't run that — I don't have a Bash tool (or any file/shell tools) available.' (stop_reason=end_turn, is_error=false) — Bash was blocked. The claude --help text confirms: '--tools <tools...>  Specify the list of available tools from the built-in set. Use "" to disable all tools'. Code at claude_code.py:242 confirmed to emit `["--allowed-tools", ",".join(inv.allowed_tools)]` — for `[]` this produces `["--allowed-tools", ""]`. The causal chain via plan_tournament_runner.py:137-138 (sets role_allowed_tools[role]=[] for _TEXT_ONLY_NO_TOOL_ROLES) → tournament/llm.py:335-336 (returns [] for text-only roles, bypassing the sentinel) → claude_code.py:242 (emits --allowed-tools "") is verified by reading all three files.

Contrast: `claude -p "Run bash: echo BASH_RAN" --tools "" --max-turns 2 --output-format json` → result says no Bash tool available. Fix: change `--allowed-tools` to `--tools` in _build_command at claude_code.py:242 for all cases when inv.allowed_tools is not None.

field_probe_findings.title: F-2: hard-task budget-churn causes 40-minute execute timeout — no delivery (P4/P5/P6 2026-06-17 re-run)
field_probe_findings.claim: Python feature/refactor/50k-scale tasks (P4/P5/P6) ran for 40-56 minutes each and hit the autodev execute 2400s hard timeout with no diff delivered. Severe churn: P5 had 59 budget cycles, 7 claude error_max_turns, qa_gate_failed (pytest collection errors), and conflict_rewrite_cap_exceeded (A2 critic-rewrite escalation failing LOUD at its cap). P4 had 5 budget-recovery cycles; P6 had 24 budget cycles and 6 tournament rounds. Root cause: tasks that require multiple files or non-trivial reasoning enter an irrecoverable churn loop that consumes the entire budget without converging on a deliverable.
field_probe_findings.evidence: P4 task_007 (~51m, 5 recoveries, timed out at 2400s, 0 WS-4 ops); P5 task_008 (~56m, 59 budget cycles, 7 error_max_turns, conflict_rewrite_cap_exceeded, timed out at 2400s, 0 WS-4 ops); P6 task_009 (~43m, 24 budget cycles, 6 tournament rounds, timed out at 2400s, 0 WS-4 ops). S3 50k-scale NOT the driver: plan tournament completed on 50k-file repo, init_plan present — delivery blocked by churn, not by scale.
field_probe_findings.repro_or_probe: Run any non-trivial Python feature or refactor task; assert execute converges and delivers within the timeout budget without exceeding budget_recovery threshold or conflict_rewrite_cap.
field_probe_findings.recommendation: Investigate convergence/budget: (1) cap budget-recovery cycles to prevent infinite churn; (2) investigate claude max_turns exhaustion and error_max_turns cascades; (3) investigate conflict_rewrite_cap interaction with A2 auto-3way; (4) add execute timeout headroom or escalate to LOUD failure before timeout.

field_probe_findings.title: F-3: benchmark harness bytes-not-JSON-serializable crash on subprocess.TimeoutExpired — FIXED
field_probe_findings.claim: When autodev execute hits the 2400s harness timeout, subprocess.TimeoutExpired.stdout/stderr are raw bytes objects. The result serializer called json.dump() on these without decoding, raising TypeError: Object of type bytes is not JSON serializable. This crashed the harness and discarded probe results rather than recording the timeout outcome.
field_probe_findings.evidence: Exposed during P4/P5/P6 runs in the 2026-06-17 re-run. Harness crashed on TimeoutExpired with TypeError rather than recording the timeout result.
field_probe_findings.repro_or_probe: Run any task that hits the 2400s timeout; assert result is recorded as timeout, not a crash.
